questions.chapter: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
questions.question_text: Which two properties define an intelligent textbook?

options.A: Cloud hosting and a conversational tutor on every page
options.B: Explicit structure stored as data, and interactive elements
options.C: A searchable glossary and a strict build that passes
options.D: Adaptive lessons and chapters generated for each reader

questions.explanation: An intelligent textbook is defined by explicit structure and interactivity. Its concepts, dependencies, and learning outcomes are stored as data that software can read and check, and it contains elements the reader operates and that report back what the reader did. A conversational tutor and per-reader lessons belong to Levels 4 and 5 of the five-level scale; they are higher levels, not the defining properties.

questions.chapter: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
questions.question_text: What is a MicroSim?

options.A: A static figure that summarizes one chapter's main ideas
options.B: A full-chapter simulation covering several related topics
options.C: A build script that checks a chapter for broken links
options.D: A small interactive simulation that demonstrates one idea

questions.explanation: A MicroSim is a small, self-contained interactive simulation, embedded in a textbook page, that demonstrates exactly one idea. The narrow scope is the point: it has one learning objective, a few controls, and a result the reader can see change, such as a slider that redraws a chart. A simulation spanning several topics breaks that rule, and a static figure gives the reader nothing to operate.

questions.chapter: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
questions.question_text: What does `mkdocs build --strict` do that an ordinary build does not?

options.A: It treats every warning as an error and stops the build
options.B: It publishes the finished site straight to GitHub Pages
options.C: It adds every page on disk to the navigation sidebar
options.D: It rewrites broken links so the build can still finish

questions.explanation: A strict site build treats every warning as an error. An ordinary build prints a warning about a broken link and finishes anyway, so the defect ships as a dead link. With `--strict` the build aborts, and the defect becomes a failed build you must fix. It does not repair links or edit the navigation for you; it only refuses to finish while warnings remain.

questions.chapter: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
questions.question_text: What is true of a Python script that uses only the standard library?

options.A: It must be compiled to a binary before the interpreter can run it
options.B: It runs on any machine with Python, with nothing installed
options.C: It can run only on the aarch64 processor architecture
options.D: It needs a conda environment to locate its modules

questions.explanation: The standard library is the set of modules that ship with Python itself, such as `platform`, `os`, and `json`. A script that imports only those modules needs no extra packages, so it runs on any machine that has Python. That portability is why the chapter's short machine report works unchanged on different systems. The interpreter runs a script from top to bottom; there is no separate compile step to perform first.

questions.chapter: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
questions.question_text: Why does the typical failure of a generative AI assistant call for a habit of verification?

options.A: The answer is plausible and fluent but slightly wrong
options.B: The answer is usually nonsense that will not run at all
options.C: The assistant refuses requests that lack enough context
options.D: The assistant returns a different command on every request

questions.explanation: The typical failure is not nonsense. It is an answer that is plausible, fluent, and slightly wrong, which makes it easy to accept without checking. The chapter's example command for listing the five largest files is a good answer, yet it would still list a large subdirectory among the files. Obvious nonsense is easy to catch; a nearly right answer is the dangerous one, so you run it on a scratch copy where you know the right result.

questions.chapter: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
questions.question_text: Why does an explicit "Topics not covered" section matter in a course description?

options.A: It raises the quality score above its 100-point maximum value
options.B: It lists the prerequisites the generators may assume
options.C: It sets the boundary that stops a model inventing content
options.D: It tells the generators which reading level and tone to write at

questions.explanation: The course description is the seed document, and every later artifact inherits its scope from it. A model asked to write about a DGX will happily write about training and fine-tuning unless the description rules those topics out, so an exclusion costs one line and prevents a chapter nobody wanted. Prerequisites and reading level are set by other sections: the prerequisites list and the target audience.

questions.chapter: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
questions.question_text: Why can "Describe how Tailscale builds an encrypted mesh" be tested when "Understand Tailscale" cannot?

options.A: The verb names an action that an observer can check
options.B: The longer wording covers more of the course content
options.C: The first objective sits at a higher Bloom level
options.D: The second objective lacks a clearly named learning outcome

questions.explanation: Bloom's Taxonomy classifies objectives by the kind of thinking they require, and each level has characteristic verbs. The verb tells you what the learner must do to show the objective was met. "Understand" gives no action to observe, while "describe" produces a description you can read and judge. The gain comes from observability, not from the length of the statement or from moving to a higher level of the taxonomy.

questions.chapter: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
questions.question_text: Why is plain text a useful property of a Markdown source file in this workflow?

options.A: It lets a browser display the file directly without any build step
options.B: It keeps a chapter's metadata hidden from the site's build tool
options.C: It prevents formatting mistakes such as a collapsed list
options.D: It lets Git diff it, a model write it, and a tool build it

questions.explanation: Markdown marks structure with a few punctuation conventions in an ordinary text file. Because the file is plain text, Git can diff it, a model can generate it, and a build tool can turn it into a web page. That combination is what lets a model write a textbook and a program check it. Plain text does not prevent mistakes: a list with no blank line before it still collapses into one paragraph.

questions.chapter: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
questions.question_text: You type `cd docs` and the shell prints nothing. Which command confirms where you are now?

options.A: `cat docs`, which prints the folder's contents as text
options.B: `pwd`, which prints the working directory's absolute path
options.C: `grep -n docs`, which prints the matching folder name
options.D: `cd docs` again, which prints the new path on the second attempt

questions.explanation: Silence from a shell command usually means success, and `cd` prints nothing when it works. The only evidence is the state that later commands see. `pwd` prints the absolute path of the working directory, so it shows directly that you are now inside `docs`; a different listing from `ls` would show it as well. `cat` prints the contents of a file, not a folder, and `grep` searches a file for a pattern.

questions.chapter: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
questions.question_text: A new chapter file exists under `docs` and the site builds, yet no reader can find the page in the sidebar. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The file's frontmatter block has no `title` entry
options.B: The iframe `src` in the page uses a wrong relative path
options.C: The page was never listed in `nav:` in `mkdocs.yml`
options.D: The site was built on a machine without GitHub Pages

questions.explanation: MkDocs navigation is the sidebar tree defined by the `nav:` block in `mkdocs.yml`. A page that exists on disk but is missing from `nav:` is still built, yet no reader can reach it from the sidebar. Adding a page is therefore two steps: create the file, then list it. A wrong iframe path causes a different symptom, a blank box inside a page that readers can already open.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
questions.question_text: In this book's convention, which way does a concept dependency edge point?

options.A: From the prerequisite to the concept that depends on it
options.B: From the dependent concept to its prerequisite
options.C: From an earlier chapter to a later chapter
options.D: From a taxonomy category to each concept inside it

questions.explanation: A concept dependency states that one concept must be understood before another, and this book writes it as an edge from the dependent concept to its prerequisite. The edge `Percent → Decimals` reads "Percent needs Decimals". Reading an edge the other way turns every prerequisite into a follow-on topic and silently inverts the whole ordering. Dependencies are a property of the subject, so they do not point from chapter to chapter.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
questions.question_text: What is a directed acyclic graph?

options.A: A graph in which every concept has exactly one prerequisite
options.B: A graph whose concepts are all connected in a single chain
options.C: A graph with undirected edges and at most one cycle
options.D: A graph whose edges have a direction and form no cycle

questions.explanation: A directed acyclic graph, or DAG, has edges with a direction and contains no cycle, where a cycle is a path that follows dependencies back to its starting concept. A learning graph must be a DAG because a cycle leaves no concept that can be learned first. A DAG does not have to be a single chain, and a concept in it may have several prerequisites or share one with another concept.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
questions.question_text: What serves as the checklist that generated chapter content is judged against?

options.A: The word count of the previous chapter in the book
options.B: The chapter header, whose concept table must all be taught
options.C: The FAQ entries that were generated for the chapter
options.D: The navigation sidebar entry that points to the chapter

questions.explanation: Chapter content is written into the chapter's `index.md` below a fixed header that lists the title, summary, concepts, and prerequisites. A generator is given that header and asked to fill in everything below the final rule. The header doubles as the checklist: every concept in its table should be taught, so a missing concept is a defect a program can find. The FAQ is generated afterward from the chapters, so it cannot be the standard.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
questions.question_text: Who may move a MicroSim from `built` to `approved`?

options.A: The generator, once the site passes a strict build
options.B: Any agent that has read the content generation guide
options.C: Only a human reviewer who has tested the MicroSim
options.D: The site build, when the sidebar dot turns green

questions.explanation: MicroSim status levels record how far a sim has progressed: `scaffold` means only a specification exists, `built` means it is implemented and awaiting review, and `approved` means it was tested and approved for learners. Only a human reviewer moves a MicroSim to `approved`; a generator may reach `built` and no further. The colored dot in the sidebar displays the status stored in the page's frontmatter. It does not set it.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
questions.question_text: Why can the same learning graph be regrouped into a different number of chapters without breaking a prerequisite?

options.A: Each taxonomy category maps to exactly one chapter
options.B: The graph stores a fixed chapter number on every concept
options.C: It stores dependencies, not an authored chapter order
options.D: Orphan concepts can be moved freely between any two chapters

questions.explanation: A learning graph is a DAG of concepts whose edges are dependencies. It does not store a chapter order; it stores what depends on what, and any order that respects those dependencies is valid. Chapters are a partition of the concepts in which no concept appears before its prerequisites. Taxonomy categories are a grouping for the author, not a teaching order, and this book's chapters deliberately cut across them.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
questions.question_text: Why does the elaboration score normalize CIS with a logarithm instead of a straight proportion?

options.A: Impact scores can be negative for the graph's terminal concepts
options.B: A logarithm places every concept in the top tier
options.C: Word counts must stay under a fixed chapter limit
options.D: CIS is heavy-tailed, so a plain ratio crushes most scores

questions.explanation: A concept's word-count target comes from its elaboration score, which divides the logarithm of its CIS plus one by the logarithm of the largest CIS plus one. The logarithm is needed because CIS is heavy-tailed: a few foundational concepts score in the thousands while 193 of the 506 concepts score 1. A straight proportion would crush the large majority to nearly zero. With the logarithm, a concept with a CIS of 36 scores about 0.46 and lands in tier B.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
questions.question_text: Why does keeping the writing rules in a file matter for small models in particular?

options.A: A rule in a file can be re-read after the context fills up
options.B: A rule in a file is enforced automatically by the build
options.C: A file lets the model skip any rules that it finds irrelevant
options.D: A file is always shorter than the same rules written in a prompt

questions.explanation: The content generation guide gathers every writing rule in one file so an agent can be told to read it first. That matters for small models because a rule that lives only in a prompt is lost when the context fills up, while a rule in a file can be re-read. The same file also makes two runs comparable, since both started from the same instructions. The build does not enforce the writing rules for the model.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
questions.question_text: Why does the book treat a word-count target as a guideline and not a quota?

options.A: The tier boundaries change from one chapter to the next
options.B: Short sections always score higher when they are reviewed
options.C: Padding to reach a number adds repetition and errors
options.D: A generator has no means of counting the words it wrote

questions.explanation: Anti-padding rules stop a generator from reaching a word target by inflating text. A model that sees "500 words" will often manufacture 500 words by restating itself, and padded text is repetitive and sometimes wrong. A target is therefore a guideline: a dense, correct section beats a padded one that reaches the number. If a section is thin, the remedy is a worked example or more technical detail, never a restatement of earlier paragraphs.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
questions.question_text: In a small graph, Q needs P, R needs P, and S needs R. Nothing depends on Q or S. What is the concept impact score of P?
questions.explanation: A concept's impact score is 1 for itself plus the scores of every concept that depends on it directly. Work from the ends: Q and S have no dependents, so each scores 1. R has one dependent, S, so R scores 1 + 1 = 2. P has dependents Q and R, so P scores 1 + 1 + 2 = 4. An answer of 2 counts only the number of direct dependents, and an answer of 3 leaves out P itself.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
questions.question_text: In a generated learning graph, the concepts with no prerequisites are advanced terms such as "Evaluation Report", and no introductory term appears among them. What does this pattern indicate?

options.A: The dependency edges were written in the reversed direction
options.B: The graph contains a cycle among its advanced concepts
options.C: The advanced concepts were put in the wrong taxonomy category
options.D: The impact scores were normalized without a logarithm

questions.explanation: A foundational concept has no prerequisites inside the graph, so learning can start there. In a correct graph these are plain, introductory terms such as Command Line Basics. If advanced terms such as "Evaluation Report" show up there instead, the edges were written backwards, which turns every prerequisite into a follow-on topic. Listing the concepts with no prerequisites is the check to run before trusting any graph. A cycle gives a different symptom: no valid teaching order exists at all.

questions.chapter: Small Language Models
questions.question_text: What is a token?

options.A: One of the learned numbers stored inside a model
options.B: A single letter or character in the model's input
options.C: A complete sentence that the model handles as one unit
options.D: The unit of text that a model reads and writes

questions.explanation: A token is the unit of text a language model reads and writes: usually a whole common word, a piece of a longer or rarer word, a number, or a punctuation mark. Models do not see letters or whole sentences; they see a sequence of tokens, each identified by a number. Because rare words split into several tokens, a sentence's token count is not its word count. The learned numbers inside a model are parameters, a different idea.

questions.chapter: Small Language Models
questions.question_text: What does it mean when a model is described as 27B?

options.A: Its weights take 27 gigabytes of memory to hold
options.B: Its context window holds 27 billion tokens
options.C: It has 27 billion learned numbers, called parameters
options.D: It was trained on 27 billion words of text

questions.explanation: A parameter is one of the learned numbers inside a model, and the parameter count is how many there are. A 27B model has 27 billion parameters that were adjusted during training and are fixed when you use it. The count is the main driver of memory and of the work per token, but it is not a size in gigabytes, and it does not tell you how well the model writes or follows a skill.

questions.chapter: Small Language Models
questions.question_text: What is inference?

options.A: Creating a model's parameters from training data
options.B: Running a trained model to produce output
options.C: Converting text into tokens before the model reads it
options.D: Adjusting a released model's weights for a new task

questions.explanation: Inference is the act of running a trained model to produce output. It is distinct from training, which creates the parameters from data once, at great expense. Inference then happens every time the model is used, and one machine can be enough for it. This course evaluates inference only; training and fine-tuning are out of scope. Converting text into tokens is the tokenizer's job, a step that comes before the model reads anything.

questions.chapter: Small Language Models
questions.question_text: What is structured output?

options.A: Prose that is organized into headings, lists, and tables
options.B: Reasoning tokens produced before a final answer
options.C: Output that conforms to a required format such as JSON
options.D: A reply that combines text with an attached image

questions.explanation: Structured output is output that conforms to a required format, such as a JSON object with named fields of given types. A downstream program reads it, so a single missing field or stray character can break the whole step. In this workload the learning graph must be a valid JSON file and a CSV file that agree, with no duplicate labels. Intermediate reasoning tokens belong to reasoning mode, and image handling belongs to multimodal models.

questions.chapter: Small Language Models
questions.question_text: Why is a mistake early in a large language model's output never revisited?

options.A: It writes one piece at a time, each built on all text before it
options.B: It drafts the whole reply first and then is unable to edit the draft
options.C: Its tokenizer discards earlier tokens to save context space
options.D: Its parameters are updated after every token it generates

questions.explanation: A large language model repeats one step: given the text so far, it assigns a probability to every possible next piece, one piece is chosen and appended, and the process repeats. Every piece depends on everything before it, so an early mistake is never revisited, only built upon. That mechanism explains both the fluency and the failures. The parameters do not change during use; they were fixed when training ended.

questions.chapter: Small Language Models
questions.question_text: How does an open-weight model differ from an open-source model?

options.A: An open-weight model cannot be run on hardware you own
options.B: An open-weight model is always free for commercial use
options.C: Its weights are public, but its training data and code usually are not
options.D: Its weights stay private while its training code and data are published

questions.explanation: An open-weight model publishes its trained parameters so anyone can download and run them. That does not mean the training data, the training code, or unrestricted rights are also public. In an open-source model the data and code are published and use is governed by an open-source license. An open-weight model's use is governed by a model license that can limit commercial use, so being able to download a model is not permission to use it for any purpose.

questions.chapter: Small Language Models
questions.question_text: In tool calling, what does the model itself do?

options.A: It emits a structured request that the harness then executes
options.B: It runs the shell command and returns the output as text
options.C: It edits files on the machine through its tokenizer
options.D: It asks the user to run the command and then paste the result back

questions.explanation: Tool calling is a model's ability to ask a program to act on its behalf. The model does not run commands itself. It writes a structured request naming a tool and its arguments, a surrounding program called the harness executes it, and the result returns to the model as new text. A language model only ever produces text, and that boundary explains both what agents can do and where the safety limits sit.

questions.chapter: Small Language Models
questions.question_text: Why are a generative AI model's mistakes harder to bound than a classifier's?

options.A: A generative model is trained on far less data
options.B: A classifier checks every label it assigns against a JSON schema
options.C: A generative model cannot be given instructions
options.D: A generative model's output has no fixed set of answers

questions.explanation: A generative AI model produces open-ended output, so there is no fixed list of possible answers. A classifier maps an input to one label from a fixed set, which bounds its mistakes: with two labels there are only two ways to be wrong. A generative model can instead fail by producing fluent text that is wrong or off-task. That unbounded failure mode is why measuring one needs the careful evaluation design taught later in the book.

questions.chapter: Small Language Models
questions.question_text: A model has a 16,000-token context window. You give it a 10,000-word document and expect a reply of up to 3,000 tokens. Using 1.33 tokens per word, does the task fit?

options.A: Yes, because 10,000 words is well under the 16,000-token window
options.B: No, because about 13,300 plus 3,000 tokens exceeds 16,000
options.C: Yes, because the reply does not count against the context window
options.D: No, because the document alone is about 16,300 tokens

questions.explanation: The context window counts both the text a model is given and the text it generates, and it is measured in tokens, not words. The document is about 10,000 × 1.33 = 13,300 tokens, which fits alone. Adding room for a 3,000-token reply brings the need to about 16,300 tokens, which is over 16,000. The document fits by itself and the task does not. Comparing words to tokens directly, or ignoring the reply, gives the wrong answer.

questions.chapter: Small Language Models
questions.question_text: On one DGX unit with 128 GB of memory, `mistral-medium-3.5:128b` downloaded and loaded, yet it was not counted as a usable small language model there. Why?

options.A: It ran at 3 tokens per second and no large context fit
options.B: Its weights could not be downloaded to the unit at all
options.C: Its license did not permit running it on local hardware
options.D: Its parameter count exceeded a fixed limit for small models

questions.explanation: The course's working definition has two parts, and a model can pass one and fail the other. This model is open-weight and could be downloaded and loaded, so it met the first test. On that unit it ran at 3 tokens per second and no context of 64,000 tokens or more fit, so it could not be served usefully. The definition is relative to the hardware, not to a parameter threshold, so the answer could change on a larger system.

questions.chapter: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
questions.question_text: What is a cloud LLM service?

options.A: A model whose weights you download and then run on your own GPU
options.B: A model registry from which open-weight files are downloaded
options.C: A local server that forwards requests when demand peaks
options.D: A model a provider runs on its servers and you reach online

questions.explanation: A cloud LLM service is a language model that a provider runs on its own servers and that you reach over the internet. You send a prompt, the provider's hardware runs inference, and the reply comes back. You never hold the model's weights and you do not operate the machine that runs it. Downloading weights and running them on your own GPU is the opposite arrangement, a local model deployment.

questions.chapter: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
questions.question_text: Which four parts make up a local model deployment?

options.A: Prompt, tokenizer, context window, and reply
options.B: API, chat subscription, agentic tool, and billing
options.C: Hardware, model weights, inference server, and harness
options.D: Privacy, sovereignty, offline operation, and pinning

questions.explanation: A local model deployment is a model you run on hardware you control, and it has four parts that stack: the hardware that holds and runs the model, the downloaded open-weight model weights, the inference server that loads the weights and exposes a local endpoint, and the harness that runs the agent loop against that endpoint. You gain control over the model, the version, and where every token goes, and you take on maintaining all four parts.

questions.chapter: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
questions.question_text: Why is a local deployment not the same as "nothing ever crosses a network"?

options.A: A provider still records the token counts for each local request
options.B: Weights and software are still downloaded from an outside host
options.C: The inference server checks its license online at every single start
options.D: Prompts are copied to a registry whenever a model is loaded

questions.explanation: Privacy here is control over who can see the data you send to and receive from a model. In a local deployment the prompt and the reply stay on your network, but the weights and software are downloaded once from a model registry, and that request is visible to whoever hosts them. What changes is that your content, the sensitive part, no longer has to leave. No provider records usage metadata for local requests.

questions.chapter: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
questions.question_text: Why is version pinning a precondition of a fair benchmark?

options.A: A pinned model generates its tokens faster than an unpinned one does
options.B: A pinned model is exempt from a provider's rate limits
options.C: Pinning removes the need to keep the weights file on disk
options.D: A result is meaningful only for the version that produced it

questions.explanation: Version pinning fixes the exact model version and software used so that results can be reproduced. Locally you pin by keeping the weights file and recording its name and checksum, so the model cannot change unless you change it. A cloud version can be requested only while it is offered. Pinning is a precondition of a fair benchmark because a result is only meaningful for the version that produced it. It has nothing to do with speed.

questions.chapter: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
questions.question_text: How does service availability differ between a cloud service and a local deployment?

options.A: Both fail at times; locally you can see and repair the fault
options.B: Only a cloud service has outages and degraded periods
options.C: A local deployment never stops once its model is loaded
options.D: Cloud outages are shorter because all usage is billed per token

questions.explanation: Service availability is the fraction of time a service is up and responsive. A cloud service has outages and degraded periods that you cannot fix and often cannot predict. A local deployment has outages too, but you can see and repair them. The difference is who holds the controls, not whether failures happen. Claiming that local systems never fail ignores the operational burden, which in this evaluation included a unit that froze during long runs.

questions.chapter: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
questions.question_text: A school district drafts material from student records that must stay on its own machines, then wants frontier-quality polish on a final summary that contains no student data. Which arrangement fits?

options.A: Cloud for both steps, under a contract covering the records
options.B: Hybrid: the records step local, the polish step in the cloud
options.C: Local for both steps, because one step uses sensitive data
options.D: Hybrid: the records step in the cloud, the polish step local

questions.explanation: A hybrid workflow uses a local model for some steps and a cloud service for others, and one way to split is by data sensitivity: confidential content stays local and non-sensitive work goes to the cloud. Here the records step must stay on the district's machines, while the polish step carries no student data and benefits from a frontier model. A hybrid is routing, not compromise: each step goes where its own requirements are best met.

questions.chapter: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
questions.question_text: You want to use a cloud-made book as the baseline for a local run. Which check helps establish that it is a control and not merely a reference?

options.A: That it used the same course description and the same skills
options.B: That it was generated more recently than the local run
options.C: That it contains more concepts than the local run produced
options.D: That it was produced on the provider's most expensive plan

questions.explanation: A cloud baseline is a reference result produced by a cloud model on the same inputs and under the same rules as the local run. Three questions test whether it is fair: did it use the same course description and the same skills, is its model version recorded, and did it get a human-reviewed process the local run did not? A baseline that fails any of these is a reference, not a control, and the comparison should say so.

questions.chapter: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
questions.question_text: A team plans to run a model at a site with no network connection and assumes no network is needed at any point. Which correction applies to the plan?

options.A: A cloud service can also run offline once a session is open
options.B: The model must reconnect each day to refresh its weights
options.C: Offline operation is impossible for a model that uses a GPU
options.D: Setup still needs a network to download the model and tools

questions.explanation: Offline operation is running a model with no network connection once it is installed. A local deployment can do this because the weights and the server are on the machine; a cloud service cannot. The setup still needs a network to download the model and tools, so offline operation describes the steady state, not the installation. The team must plan how the weights and software reach the machine before it goes offline.

questions.chapter: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
questions.question_text: A benchmark result recorded against a specific cloud model can no longer be reproduced, and requests to that model are now answered by a newer one. What is the cause?

options.A: The account reached a rate limit that capped its tokens for the day
options.B: The provider deprecated that model version on its schedule
options.C: The service had an outage during the original benchmark run
options.D: The workflow became locked in to the provider's formats

questions.explanation: Model deprecation is a provider's retirement of a model version, after which requests to it fail or are redirected to a newer one. A workflow built on that model changes behavior or breaks on the provider's schedule, not yours, and a benchmark result recorded against it can no longer be reproduced. A rate limit or an outage would stall or interrupt a run, but neither one replaces the model that answers.

questions.chapter: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
questions.question_text: A team runs a task through a cloud provider's agentic framework and credits the result entirely to the provider's model. What does that attribution overlook?

options.A: A framework's output cannot be scored against a rubric
options.B: A framework always lowers the quality of its model
options.C: The observed quality reflects the model and framework together
options.D: A local model cannot be wrapped with tools, memory, or a planning loop

questions.explanation: An agentic framework wraps a language model with tools, memory, and a planning loop so it can carry out multi-step tasks. The model supplies the language ability, and the framework supplies the structure that lets it act. Many frameworks are tied to a provider's models and sold with them, so the quality you observe is the quality of the model and the framework together. Crediting everything to the model ignores half of what produced the result.

questions.chapter: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
questions.question_text: What does a buyer of an NVIDIA DGX system receive?

options.A: A GPU card that the buyer installs in an existing server chassis
options.B: A cloud subscription that rents GPUs by the hour
options.C: A set of drivers to download for any Linux computer
options.D: A complete machine with hardware, OS, and GPU software matched

questions.explanation: NVIDIA DGX is NVIDIA's line of systems built for AI work, sold as complete machines with the hardware, the operating system, and the GPU software already matched to each other. The driver, the compute libraries, and a container runtime arrive installed and known to work together, which removes the most common source of setup trouble on a self-assembled GPU server. The line ranges from a desktop box to an eight-GPU rack server.

questions.chapter: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
questions.question_text: What is unified memory?

options.A: Memory mounted on the GPU's own board for its sole use
options.B: Disk space the system uses when its RAM runs out
options.C: A single memory pool shared by the CPU and the GPU
options.D: The combined memory of several GPUs in a single chassis

questions.explanation: Unified memory is a single pool of memory shared by the CPU and the GPU, so both read and write the same physical chips. The GB10 uses it: its 128 GB is the whole of the machine's memory, and the GPU has no memory of its own. Memory mounted on the GPU's own board is dedicated GPU memory, the arrangement on a rack DGX, where each GPU's pool is a separate hard limit.

questions.chapter: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
questions.question_text: What is DGX OS?

options.A: An Ubuntu-based Linux with NVIDIA's components pre-installed
options.B: A firmware layer that runs beneath the Linux kernel
options.C: A container image that holds only an inference server
options.D: A Windows-based system tuned for GPU workstations

questions.explanation: DGX OS is NVIDIA's operating system for DGX systems: a customized Linux distribution, based on Ubuntu, with the NVIDIA driver, CUDA, the container runtime, and system tuning installed and tested together. The unit in this evaluation runs DGX OS 7.4 on Ubuntu 24.04. The practical meaning is that ordinary Ubuntu instructions work, and that NVIDIA's own components are already present and compatible with each other.

questions.chapter: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
questions.question_text: Why does a GPU suit language-model inference?

options.A: It stores model weights far more compactly than system RAM is able to
options.B: It executes x86_64 and aarch64 programs equally well
options.C: It reads model files from disk faster than a CPU can
options.D: It runs many simple operations at once, suiting matrix arithmetic

questions.explanation: A GPU is a processor built to run many simple operations at once. It began as hardware for drawing images, and its design turned out to suit the matrix arithmetic that neural networks consist of. A language model generating text is almost entirely matrix arithmetic, so a GPU does it far faster than a CPU can. Storage and compactness are not the reason. Without a GPU, the models in this course would take minutes per sentence.

questions.chapter: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
questions.question_text: Why does a single power-draw number mislead for a GPU-heavy machine?

options.A: Draw under load far exceeds draw at rest, so workload matters
options.B: Power draw is fixed by the chip's thermal design power
options.C: Electricity is the largest cost of owning the machine
options.D: The GPU reports power only when its memory is dedicated

questions.explanation: Power draw is the electrical power the system consumes, in watts. A GPU-heavy machine draws far more under load than at rest, so a single number misleads, and a measurement needs the workload that produced it. Thermal design power is a cooling specification, not a measurement of draw. Electricity is also a small part of the cost of owning this machine: under $120 a year in the book's estimate.

questions.chapter: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
questions.question_text: What does the `CUDA Version` shown in the first line of `nvidia-smi` output mean?

options.A: The version of the CUDA toolkit installed on the machine
options.B: The newest CUDA runtime the installed driver can support
options.C: The compute capability assigned to the GPU generation
options.D: The oldest CUDA runtime that programs are allowed to use

questions.explanation: CUDA has two parts that are easy to confuse. The CUDA runtime is the set of libraries a program is built against, and it ships inside the programs that use it. The CUDA version in the `nvidia-smi` header is the newest runtime the installed driver can support, not the version of any toolkit on the machine. The driver therefore sets a ceiling: a framework built at or below that version runs, and one built above it does not.

questions.chapter: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
questions.question_text: You copy an install command from a tutorial. The download completes on your unit but the file fails when you run it, and `uname -m` prints `aarch64`. What should you do?

options.A: Find the build whose name says `arm64` or `aarch64`
options.B: Retry the same download until the file runs correctly
options.C: Update the NVIDIA driver to a newer release first
options.D: Free some disk space and run the downloaded file again

questions.explanation: CPU architecture is the instruction set a processor executes, and x86_64 and aarch64 are not compatible: a program compiled for one cannot run on the other without translation. Many install pages offer an x86_64 file first, and a download that completes on an aarch64 machine still fails when you run it. The fix is to find the aarch64 build, whose name says `arm64` or `aarch64`, not to retry the same file.

questions.chapter: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
questions.question_text: A model's weights take 120 GB. A server has four GPUs with 80 GB of dedicated memory each and plenty of system RAM. How must the model be placed?

options.A: On one GPU, with the overflow held in system RAM
options.B: Split across at least two of the GPUs
options.C: In system RAM, with the GPUs doing the arithmetic
options.D: On one GPU, after the driver has been updated

questions.explanation: Dedicated GPU memory belongs to one GPU alone, and a model placed on that GPU must fit entirely in it, because the GPU cannot use system RAM at full speed. Each 80 GB pool is a hard limit. A 120 GB model cannot go on one of these GPUs however much system RAM the server has, so it must be split across at least two, and the software that does the splitting is a setup step of its own.

questions.chapter: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
questions.question_text: A 30 GB model file is read from an NVMe drive at 2 GB per second. About how long does the model take to load?

options.A: About 2 seconds
options.B: About 7 seconds
options.C: About 10 seconds
options.D: About 15 seconds

questions.explanation: Storage read speed is how many bytes per second the drive delivers, and for a model it sets the load time, the delay between asking for a model and being able to use it. The relation is simple division: 30 GB read at 2 GB per second takes 15 seconds. A server that unloads an idle model and reloads it on the next request pays this cost each time, which is why a fast drive matters.

questions.chapter: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
questions.question_text: A program reports that it found no CUDA device, yet `nvidia-smi` lists the GPU and a driver version. Where does the problem most likely lie?

options.A: In the GPU hardware, which has failed and must be replaced
options.B: In the driver, which must be reinstalled before anything else can run
options.C: In a layer above the driver, such as the framework's CUDA build
options.D: In the storage layer, which cannot hold the model file

questions.explanation: The NVIDIA driver is the software that lets the operating system and programs talk to the GPU. The first diagnostic step for a "no CUDA device" report is always to run `nvidia-smi`. If it lists the GPU and a driver version, the driver works, and the problem is in what is built on top of it, such as a framework built for a CUDA runtime above the driver's ceiling. Reinstalling the driver would repair a layer that is not broken.

questions.chapter: Cost, Price, and Quality
questions.question_text: In this book's terms, what is cost?

options.A: What a provider charges a customer for a service
options.B: What you pay to own and operate something
options.C: How good the output of a model turns out to be
options.D: What a seller adds to a book's price as profit

questions.explanation: Cost is what you pay to own and operate something: the money, time, and effort that go out of your organization to produce a result. It belongs to whoever bears it. For a book generated on your own hardware, it is the share of hardware, setup labor, electricity, and administration that the book uses up. What a provider charges is a price, and how good the output is is quality. A comparison needs all three kept apart.

questions.chapter: Cost, Price, and Quality
questions.question_text: Which statement describes fixed costs?

options.A: They rise in proportion to the number of books produced
options.B: They are charged by a provider for each million tokens
options.C: They stay the same regardless of how much you produce
options.D: They are incurred only in the year hardware is purchased

questions.explanation: Fixed costs stay the same regardless of how much you produce. The unit's depreciation, the setup labor, and the monthly operations labor are the same in a year with 10 books and a year with 150, so a machine that sits idle costs what a busy machine costs. In the reference case they are about $8,160 of the $8,275 a year. Costs that rise with production, such as electricity used while generating, are variable costs.

questions.chapter: Cost, Price, and Quality
questions.question_text: Why is a cost model without a quality statement incomplete?

options.A: Quality determines the electricity that a run consumes
options.B: Quality sets the price a provider charges per token
options.C: Poor output must be redone or reviewed at further cost
options.D: Quality is fixed by the purchase price of the hardware

questions.explanation: Quality is how good the output is. It is neither a cost nor a price, and it is the term most often left out of a comparison. A local model that costs half as much and writes a learning graph with 40 duplicate labels has not saved half. It has produced something that must be redone or reviewed at further cost. That is why a cost figure needs a quality statement beside it before it supports a decision.

questions.chapter: Cost, Price, and Quality
questions.question_text: Why does the cost per book rise from $53 to $263 when utilization falls from 50% to 10%?

options.A: The machine draws more idle power at low utilization
options.B: The hardware depreciates faster when it sits unused
options.C: Operations labor grows as fewer books are generated
options.D: The same fixed cost is shared among far fewer books

questions.explanation: Utilization rate is the share of available time the machine spends doing useful work, and it is the lever that fixed costs ride on. At 50% the unit produces 156 books a year at $53 each; at 10% it produces 31 at $263 each. The cost does not rise because the machine got worse. It rises because the same fixed cost, about $8,275 a year, is shared among a fifth as many books.

questions.chapter: Cost, Price, and Quality
questions.question_text: Why was every tool in this evaluation installed into a home directory from a release archive?

options.A: The account had no administrator privileges for system installs
options.B: Release archives run faster than system-wide packages do
options.C: DGX OS forbids installing software outside home directories
options.D: The Administrator required all tools to run inside Docker

questions.explanation: Administrator privileges are the right to change system-wide settings: installing software for all users, changing the driver, opening network ports, and managing accounts. The benchmark account had none, so every tool was installed into a home directory from a release archive and nothing was changed system-wide. Steps that did need those rights, such as joining the `docker` group, were requests to the Administrator, and each request has a delay.

questions.chapter: Cost, Price, and Quality
questions.question_text: A unit's annual cost is $8,275 and it generates for 4,380 hours a year, so each generating hour costs about $1.89. What does a book that needs 40 hours of generation cost?

options.A: About $47
options.B: About $53
options.C: About $76
options.D: About $207

questions.explanation: A cost model is a written set of assumptions and formulas that turns inputs into a cost figure. Here the annual cost of $8,275 divided by 4,380 generating hours gives $1.89 per generating hour, and 40 hours × $1.89 is about $76. The $53 figure belongs to the reference book, which takes 28 hours. Dividing the annual cost by 40 confuses hours per book with books per year and gives a meaningless $207.

questions.chapter: Cost, Price, and Quality
questions.question_text: A book costs $40 to produce. Which price gives the seller a 20% profit margin?
questions.explanation: Profit margin is the share of a price that is profit: price minus cost, divided by price. For a 20% margin the price is the cost divided by 0.80, so $40 ÷ 0.80 is $50, and the $10 profit is 20% of that price. Multiplying the cost by 1.20 gives $48, which is a 20% markup, measured against cost. That price yields a margin of only 16.7%, less than the seller intended.

questions.chapter: Cost, Price, and Quality
questions.question_text: A unit generates for 2,000 hours a year at 150 W and idles for the other 6,760 hours at 40 W. About how much energy does it use in a year?

options.A: About 570 kWh
options.B: About 300 kWh
options.C: About 832 kWh
options.D: About 1,314 kWh

questions.explanation: Electricity cost is energy consumed times the price of energy, and a machine that is on but not generating still draws idle power, so yearly energy has two terms. Generating: 2,000 h × 150 W = 300,000 Wh. Idle: 6,760 h × 40 W = 270,400 Wh. Together that is 570,400 Wh, or about 570 kWh. Counting only the generating hours gives 300 kWh and leaves out nearly half of the energy.

questions.chapter: Cost, Price, and Quality
questions.question_text: In the reference case, changing the hardware price moves the cost per book by about ten percent, while changing operations labor moves it by up to a factor of two. What does this pattern tell a planner?

options.A: The hardware price should be negotiated before anything else
options.B: The labor estimate deserves more scrutiny than the hardware price
options.C: Both assumptions should be varied together to save time
options.D: The cost model is too unreliable to support any decision

questions.explanation: Sensitivity analysis changes one assumption at a time and records how the output moves, so you learn which assumptions the answer depends on. Doubling operations labor raises the cost per book from $53 to $81 and removing it drops it to $25, while hardware price moves it by about ten percent. The ranking shows where attention belongs: on the labor estimate. Varying two assumptions together would hide which one moved the answer.

questions.chapter: Cost, Price, and Quality
questions.question_text: A break-even calculation returns 426 books a year against a $20 alternative, but one unit can produce only 156 books a year. What does this result mean?

options.A: The unit breaks even once demand grows to 426 books
options.B: The formula is invalid whenever the price is below $50
options.C: The unit's variable cost per book has been overstated
options.D: One unit cannot break even at any volume it can reach

questions.explanation: Break-even volume is the production level at which two options cost the same: the fixed cost divided by the saving on each book. A result above what the machine can produce is not a target to grow into. It means that against that alternative, one unit does not break even at any volume it can reach. The formula gives no warning, so always compare the result with capacity: generating hours divided by hours per book.

questions.chapter: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
questions.question_text: What distinguishes a mesh VPN from a hub-and-spoke VPN?

options.A: Each device connects directly to the others, with no central hub
options.B: All traffic passes through one central server that someone must run
options.C: The router forwards a public port to each member device
options.D: Devices connect without encryption inside a private range

questions.explanation: A mesh VPN is one in which every device can connect directly to every other device, with no central machine that all traffic must pass through. A conventional VPN is hub-and-spoke: traffic between two devices goes through one server, and if the hub fails everything goes down. In a mesh the path from laptop to DGX is one hop, and the coordination service that sets up connections carries no traffic.

questions.chapter: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
questions.question_text: In an SSH key pair, which key is the secret, and where does the other one go?

options.A: The public key is secret; the private key goes in `known_hosts`
options.B: Both keys are secret and both stay in `~/.ssh` on the laptop
options.C: The private key is secret; the public key goes in `authorized_keys`
options.D: The private key is copied to the server; the public key stays on the laptop

questions.explanation: An SSH key pair is two linked files. The private key stays on your machine and is the secret: anyone who holds it can log in as you. The public key is safe to share and goes into the server's `authorized_keys` file. The server uses it to check that you hold the matching private key, without the private key ever crossing the network. `known_hosts` is a different file, where the client stores server keys.

questions.chapter: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
questions.question_text: What is a tailnet?

options.A: A relay server that forwards encrypted packets between peers
options.B: A private network of devices and users under one Tailscale account
options.C: A WireGuard configuration file listing each peer's public key
options.D: A public address range that home routers assign to devices

questions.explanation: A tailnet is a private network of devices and users managed together under one Tailscale account or organization. Its devices get stable private addresses from a reserved range that starts `100.` and names that resolve only inside the tailnet. Only members can reach one another, and the tailnet's administrator controls who is a member and what each may reach. A relay that forwards encrypted packets is a DERP server, a separate idea.

questions.chapter: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
questions.question_text: Why can two machines behind two home routers not simply connect to each other?

options.A: Home routers block all encrypted traffic by default
options.B: Each router drops incoming connections it has no record of
options.C: The two machines are assigned the same private address
options.D: SSH servers refuse logins that arrive from another network

questions.explanation: A home router performs NAT: many private devices share one public address, and the router keeps a table of the conversations that started from inside. A reply to such a conversation is let back in. A new connection that arrives unprompted has no entry in the table, so the router drops it. Two machines behind two routers each look like an unsolicited connection to the other's router, so neither gets through.

questions.chapter: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
questions.question_text: What does Tailscale add to WireGuard?

options.A: Automatic key distribution, address discovery, and NAT traversal
options.B: A stronger encryption scheme that replaces WireGuard's own
options.C: A central server through which all device traffic is routed
options.D: Password-based login for devices that have no key pair

questions.explanation: WireGuard secures a connection and leaves finding and keying the peers to you: someone must generate keys, copy public keys, and know each peer's reachable address. Tailscale builds a WireGuard mesh automatically. It generates each device's keys, distributes the public keys, discovers current addresses, and arranges the connection across the routers. It does not replace WireGuard's encryption, and its coordination service carries no device traffic.

questions.chapter: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
questions.question_text: Why does the privacy of your prompts not depend on trusting the coordination service?

options.A: Data travels encrypted between the devices, not through the service
options.B: The service deletes every prompt as soon as it has finished forwarding it
options.C: The service runs on hardware that the tailnet's owner controls
options.D: Prompts are sent only while the coordination service is offline

questions.explanation: Tailscale separates two jobs. The coordination plane exchanges setup information between each device and the service: public keys, addresses, and access rules. The data plane carries your SSH sessions, prompts, and replies directly between the two devices, encrypted by WireGuard, and it does not pass through the service. The service learns identities, keys, and addresses, and nothing about the content. It knows who talked to whom and never hears the conversation.

questions.chapter: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
questions.question_text: You want to confirm that key login works before a script depends on it. Which command is the standard test?

options.A: `ssh-copy-id <user>@<dgx-host>`, then enter the password
options.B: `ssh <user>@<dgx-host> hostname`, with no extra options
options.C: `ssh -o BatchMode=yes <user>@<dgx-host> hostname`
options.D: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519`, then read the files in `~/.ssh`

questions.explanation: BatchMode tells the SSH client never to prompt for a password or passphrase and to fail at once if a prompt would be needed. The command prints the machine's name if key login works and `Permission denied` if the key is not installed or is not the one offered. A plain `ssh` can fall back to asking for a password and appear to work, which hides a broken key, so it is not a reliable test.

questions.chapter: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
questions.question_text: While `ssh -N -L 11434:127.0.0.1:11434 <user>@<dgx-host>` runs, where does a request to port 11434 on the laptop go?

options.A: To port 11434 on the laptop itself, since `127.0.0.1` is local
options.B: To port 22 on the DGX, where the SSH server answers it
options.C: To the coordination service, which then relays it to the DGX
options.D: To the model server on the DGX, through the SSH connection

questions.explanation: An SSH port forward carries traffic for one port through an SSH connection. `-N` holds the tunnel open without running a remote command, and `-L` takes the form `local-port:destination:destination-port`. The destination is resolved on the remote side, so `127.0.0.1` there means the DGX itself, not the laptop. A request to port 11434 on the laptop therefore reaches the model server on the DGX, traveling inside the encrypted SSH connection.

questions.chapter: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
questions.question_text: A status listing shows that your laptop reaches a DGX unit through a DERP relay instead of a direct connection. What should you conclude?

options.A: The relay can read the session, so stop sending prompts
options.B: The coordination service is now carrying all of the traffic
options.C: The unit's device key has expired and must be renewed
options.D: The traffic is still encrypted by the devices but is slower

questions.explanation: A DERP relay is the fallback when a direct path cannot be opened, for example when a firewall blocks outgoing UDP. The packets are already encrypted by the devices, so the relay forwards data it cannot read. A relayed connection is slower because the traffic takes a longer route, and the clients keep probing and switch to a direct path as soon as one becomes possible. The coordination service still carries no traffic.

questions.chapter: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
questions.question_text: The person running the benchmark cannot change the DGX's router, and the machine must not be reachable by strangers. Why does port forwarding fail both constraints?

options.A: It cannot carry SSH traffic, which a mesh VPN can carry
options.B: It needs a router change and exposes the login port publicly
options.C: It requires a central hub that someone has to run and keep patched
options.D: It prevents scripts from connecting when no person is present to log in

questions.explanation: Remote access can be arranged by port forwarding, a conventional VPN, or a mesh VPN, and they differ in what they expose. Port forwarding needs a change on the DGX's router, which the evaluator cannot make, and it opens the machine's login service to everyone on the internet, where guessing attempts arrive within minutes. Running a hub is the drawback of a conventional VPN. Only the mesh VPN passed every constraint in this evaluation.

questions.chapter: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
questions.question_text: What is a Python environment?

options.A: A server that hosts packages for conda to download
options.B: A file that lists packages with optional version pins
options.C: A system-wide Python shared by every project on a machine
options.D: A self-contained directory with an interpreter and its packages

questions.explanation: A Python environment is a self-contained directory that holds a Python interpreter and the packages installed for it, together with a script that points your shell at them. Activating it puts its interpreter and packages first on your path, so `python` runs that interpreter and `import` finds those packages and no others. Because it is only a directory, you never repair a broken one: you delete it and rebuild it from the specification.

questions.chapter: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
questions.question_text: What is Miniforge?

options.A: A commercial Python distribution that requires a paid license
options.B: A pip replacement that installs only Python packages
options.C: A minimal conda installer that defaults to the conda-forge channel
options.D: A build tool that compiles wheels for aarch64 machines

questions.explanation: Miniforge is a minimal installer for conda that is set up to use the community-maintained conda-forge channel by default, and it is the installer this course uses. The alternative, a distribution from a commercial vendor, brings a default channel whose licensing terms can require a paid license for larger organizations. A book whose readers work in unknown organizations should not depend on that, which is why Miniforge was chosen.

questions.chapter: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
questions.question_text: Two documentation tools each pin a different version of the same package. Why does giving each tool its own environment fix the conflict?

options.A: Each environment downloads packages from a different channel
options.B: Conda merges the two versions into one compatible build
options.C: pip is allowed to override conda inside a shared environment
options.D: Neither tool then has to agree with the other on one version

questions.explanation: Environment isolation keeps each environment separate so that a change in one cannot affect another. A package can exist in only one version at a time in one place, so two tools that pin different versions cannot both be satisfied in a shared environment: installing the second breaks the first. The fix was not a cleverer install. With one environment per tool, neither has to agree with the other.

questions.chapter: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
questions.question_text: Why does the book advise installing with conda first and doing any pip installs last?

options.A: pip cannot run until conda has been removed from the path
options.B: pip can replace a conda package, leaving conda's record wrong
options.C: conda refuses to activate an environment that pip has touched
options.D: pip installs Python itself, which must follow the packages

questions.explanation: Conda versus pip is a question of scope: pip handles only Python packages, while conda handles Python itself, non-Python libraries, and tools. The rule is to install with conda first, use pip only for what conda does not have, and do the pip installs last. Going back and forth lets pip replace a package that conda installed, and conda's record is then wrong about what is present in the environment.

questions.chapter: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
questions.question_text: Why is `conda env export --from-history` portable across architectures when a full export is not?

options.A: It records exact builds, which are identical on every platform
options.B: It records only requested packages, so conda resolves the rest
options.C: It converts each build string to the target architecture
options.D: It leaves out the channel, so any server can supply packages

questions.explanation: The two export forms record different things. A full `conda env export` lists every package with its exact build, and builds are specific to one platform, so rebuilding on another platform fails with packages that cannot be found. Exporting with `--from-history` records only the packages you asked for, and conda resolves the rest for the new platform. The price is that each dependency resolves to whatever is current unless you pin it yourself.

questions.chapter: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
questions.question_text: You need a new environment named `probe`, built from conda-forge, with Python pinned to 3.12 and `psutil` installed. Which command does this?

options.A: `conda activate probe -c conda-forge python=3.12 psutil`
options.B: `conda env remove -n probe -c conda-forge python=3.12`
options.C: `conda create -c probe -n conda-forge python psutil=3.12`
options.D: `conda create -n probe -c conda-forge python=3.12 psutil`

questions.explanation: The conda create command makes a new environment. `-n probe` names it, `-c conda-forge` names the channel to search, and everything after is the packages to install, with a version after an equals sign as a pin. Writing `python=3.12` fixes the major and minor version, and `psutil` is left unpinned. `conda activate` only switches the shell into an existing environment, and `conda env remove` deletes one.

questions.chapter: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
questions.question_text: A script running in a non-interactive shell fails at the line `conda activate dgx` with a "command not found" error. What should the script do instead?

options.A: Use `conda run -n dgx <command>` or the full executable path
options.B: Put `sudo` in front of the `conda activate dgx` line
options.C: Reinstall Miniforge so that the activate function exists
options.D: Run `conda env remove -n dgx` and create the environment again

questions.explanation: The `conda activate` function is defined by your shell's startup files, so a script or an agent running in a non-interactive shell may fail with a permission or "command not found" error. The fix is to call the environment's executables by their full path, or to use `conda run -n dgx <command>`. Nothing is wrong with the environment or the installer, so removing or reinstalling either one does not address the cause.

questions.chapter: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
questions.question_text: After you install PyTorch on the DGX, `import torch` succeeds. How do you confirm that this build can use the GPU?

options.A: Check that `torch.cuda.is_available()` returns `True`
options.B: Check that `import torch` finishes without any error
options.C: Check that `conda list` shows a `torch` package entry
options.D: Check that `uname -m` prints `aarch64` on the machine

questions.explanation: CUDA-enabled PyTorch is the build compiled to use an NVIDIA GPU. The default install on some platforms is a CPU-only build, and it imports without any error, so a successful `import torch` proves nothing about the GPU. `torch.cuda.is_available()` returns `True` only if the driver and a GPU are usable, and `torch.version.cuda` is `None` for a CPU-only build. A model that silently runs on the CPU looks like a performance problem when it is an install problem.

questions.chapter: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
questions.question_text: On an aarch64 DGX, a `pip install` of one package runs for a long time, asks for a compiler, and then fails. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The environment's Python version was pinned to 3.12
options.B: The package was requested from the conda-forge channel
options.C: The package has no aarch64 wheel, so pip built from source
options.D: The NVIDIA driver is older than the package's CUDA build requires

questions.explanation: A wheel is a built Python package, and an architecture-specific wheel is built for one processor architecture, named in its filename. On an aarch64 machine pip accepts only wheels whose last tag is `aarch64`. If a package publishes only x86_64 wheels, pip falls back to compiling it from source, which is slow, needs a compiler, and can fail. That pattern points to a missing wheel, not to the Python pin or the GPU driver.

questions.chapter: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
questions.question_text: After you rebuild `environment.yml` into a throwaway environment, the `diff` of the two package lists shows three differing lines. What do those lines indicate?

options.A: The rebuild ran on a different processor architecture
options.B: The original environment is corrupted and must be removed at once
options.C: Unpinned packages resolved to newer releases; pin them next
options.D: The specification named a package channel that no longer exists

questions.explanation: An environment rebuild creates the environment again from its specification and compares it with the original. A specification you have never rebuilt from is an unverified claim, and the rebuild is the test. An empty `diff` means the rebuild matches. A few differing lines are the packages that were not pinned and resolved to a newer release, and they are exactly what to pin next. They do not mean the original environment is damaged.

questions.chapter: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
questions.question_text: Which two conda-forge packages does this course's Tailscale installation need?

options.A: `tailscale`, the client, and `tailscaled`, the daemon
options.B: `tailscale`, the client, and `wireguard`, the protocol
options.C: `tailscaled`, the daemon, and `openssh`, the login server
options.D: `tailscale`, the client, and `magicdns`, the name service

questions.explanation: Tailscale installation here means installing the open-source command-line client and its daemon into a dedicated conda environment, so the tooling for reaching the DGX is isolated and removable. The two conda-forge packages are `tailscale`, the client, and `tailscaled`, the daemon. The client does nothing without the daemon, so install both at the same version. The test is that `tailscale version` and `tailscaled --version` print the same number.

questions.chapter: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
questions.question_text: What is a read-only inventory?

options.A: A backup of the machine's disk taken before any install
options.B: A list of the packages in a conda environment, with builds
options.C: A survey made with commands that change nothing on the machine
options.D: A log of every command an administrator has run on the unit

questions.explanation: A read-only inventory is a survey of a machine's hardware and software made with commands that change nothing and need no administrator rights. It is the first thing to do on any machine you do not know, and the right first step on one that belongs to someone else, because it answers the hardware questions without asking permission to install anything. Commands such as `uname -srm`, `free -h`, and `df -h /` print a few lines and write nothing.

questions.chapter: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
questions.question_text: What does MagicDNS provide?

options.A: A name for each tailnet device that resolves to its private address
options.B: A public DNS record that lets anyone find the device online
options.C: A pre-generated credential that joins a device with no browser sign-in
options.D: A policy document listing who may reach which machine and port

questions.explanation: MagicDNS gives every device in a tailnet a name that resolves to its private address, so you type a name and not an address. Names are stable even if the address changes, so a script written against the name keeps working. A short name resolves only from inside the tailnet, and names appear as placeholders in anything published. A pre-generated credential is an auth key, and a policy document is an access control list.

questions.chapter: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
questions.question_text: Why must a Tailscale auth key be handled like a password?

options.A: It encrypts every packet exchanged inside the tailnet
options.B: It lets a device join the tailnet with no one signing in
options.C: It grants administrator rights on every machine in the tailnet
options.D: It can never be limited to one use or given an expiry

questions.explanation: A Tailscale auth key is a pre-generated credential that lets a device join a tailnet without a person signing in through a browser. It exists for machines nobody sits at. Because it is equivalent to a password for joining the network, it must never go in a repository, a chat, a screenshot, or a log. Keys can be limited to one use and can expire, and a key that expires soon and works once is the one to prefer.

questions.chapter: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
questions.question_text: Why is `tailscale ping` a stronger test than `tailscale status`?

options.A: Ping proves that key-based SSH login works without a prompt
options.B: Ping restarts the daemon whenever a device shows as offline
options.C: Ping shows packets reach the device; status only lists it
options.D: Ping checks the SSH server; status checks the access rules

questions.explanation: `tailscale status` lists the devices you can see with their address, owner, and connection state, so it shows that a device is listed. Tailscale ping tests the connection at the tailnet layer, below SSH: it sends a probe and reports the path used and the time taken, which shows that packets actually reach the device. Neither one proves the login works. That takes the third step, an SSH command run with BatchMode.

questions.chapter: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
questions.question_text: Why is piping a script over SSH the right method for an inventory?

options.A: It is read from standard input, so nothing is written to disk
options.B: The script runs with administrator rights on the remote machine
options.C: The script is installed permanently, so later runs start faster
options.D: The output is saved on the DGX, where the administrator can read it

questions.explanation: Piping a script over SSH runs a local file on a remote machine without copying it there first. The shell on the DGX reads the script from its standard input, so nothing is written to the machine's disk, and the output is saved on your own machine. That suits an inventory because it leaves no trace and needs no permission to write anywhere. It does not grant administrator rights.

questions.chapter: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
questions.question_text: `tailscale status` reports that it cannot connect to the daemon. What should you do first?

options.A: Ask the administrator to restart the DGX unit
options.B: Sign in again with the account that was invited
options.C: Reboot the home router to clear its NAT table
options.D: Check that `tailscaled` is running and restart it

questions.explanation: The Tailscale daemon is the background process that creates the network interface, holds the encryption keys, and maintains the connections; the client only talks to it. If `tailscale status` cannot connect to the daemon, the cause is almost always that `tailscaled` is not running, for example after a reboot or a closed tab. Restart it in its own tab, with `sudo` and the full path to the binary, before suspecting the DGX, the router, or your account.

questions.chapter: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
questions.question_text: After you run `tailscale up` and sign in, `tailscale status` lists only your own laptop. What should you check?

options.A: Whether the DGX's device key expired 180 days ago
options.B: Whether you signed in with the account that was invited
options.C: Whether `tailscaled` was started with the full binary path
options.D: Whether your SSH public key was installed with `ssh-copy-id`

questions.explanation: Tailscale authentication proves who you are to the coordination service so that your device is added to the right tailnet. Signing in with a different account than the one the administrator invited creates or joins a different tailnet, and the DGX will not appear in your device list. If the listing shows only your own laptop, compare the account on the sign-in page with the one the invitation was sent to. An expired key would show a listed device as offline.

questions.chapter: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
questions.question_text: Before a large model download, you want to know how much disk space is free and whether your account is in the `docker` group. Which pair of commands answers both?

options.A: `free -h` and `docker --version`
options.B: `lscpu` and `uname -srm`
options.C: `df -h /` and `id -nG`
options.D: `nvidia-smi` and `free -h`

questions.explanation: The Linux inventory commands each answer one question and write nothing. `df -h /` reports the disk's size and free space, and `id -nG` lists your groups, which shows whether `docker` is among them. `free -h` reports memory, not disk, and `docker --version` only shows whether Docker is present. Running these before a long download is how you learn in five minutes whether a plan is possible.

questions.chapter: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
questions.question_text: In the three-step connectivity test, `tailscale status` lists the DGX and `tailscale ping` gets replies, but the BatchMode SSH command prints `Permission denied`. Which layer is at fault?

options.A: Your Tailscale daemon or your account
options.B: The network path between the two routers
options.C: The tailnet's access control list
options.D: The SSH server or your key

questions.explanation: The connectivity test has three steps, each proving something the previous did not, so a failure tells you which layer to inspect. Status passing shows the device is listed and not offline, which clears your daemon and account. Ping passing shows packets reach the device, which clears the network path and the access rules. A failure at the third step, the BatchMode login, therefore points to the SSH server or your key.

questions.chapter: Python Hardware Probes
questions.question_text: What is a hardware probe?

options.A: A specification sheet that the hardware's vendor has published
options.B: A small, read-only measurement of one fact about a machine
options.C: A stress test that loads the GPU until it throttles
options.D: A background service that restarts a frozen machine

questions.explanation: A hardware probe is a small, read-only measurement of one fact about a machine: how many cores it has, how much memory is free, which GPU is installed. The word "measurement" matters. A probe reads the value from the machine, so it reports what is true now, whatever the specification sheet or the last person's notes say.
