It has three parts: the question, the source it reads, and the form of the answer.

questions.chapter: Python Hardware Probes
questions.question_text: What does the absence of the `nvidia-smi` command on a machine usually mean?

options.A: The GPU has overheated and shut itself down
options.B: The machine uses unified memory for its GPU
options.C: The NVIDIA driver is not installed on the machine
options.D: The account lacks administrator privileges

questions.explanation: `nvidia-smi`, the NVIDIA System Management Interface, is the command-line tool that reports a GPU's state. It is installed with the driver, so its presence on a machine is itself a probe: no `nvidia-smi` usually means no driver. Unified memory shows up differently, as GPU memory fields that come back as `Not Supported` or `[N/A]` from a tool that is present and working.

questions.chapter: Python Hardware Probes
questions.question_text: Why is `MemAvailable` the number to watch in the RAM probe, and not `MemTotal`?

options.A: It is what a new program could use without pushing others out
options.B: It is the only figure the kernel reports in gibibytes
options.C: It includes the dedicated memory of every GPU on every kind of system
options.D: It stays constant while a model server is running

questions.explanation: The RAM probe reads `/proc/meminfo`. `MemTotal` is all the memory the system can use, and `MemAvailable` is what a new program could use without pushing others out. Available is the number to watch, because a large total with little available is a machine about to struggle. On a unified-memory machine it is also the figure that model fit is judged against, since the GPU has no memory of its own.

questions.chapter: Python Hardware Probes
questions.question_text: Why should a script avoid parsing the table that `nvidia-smi` prints when run with no arguments?

options.A: The table leaves out the GPU's temperature and power
options.B: The table is printed only when the driver is missing
options.C: The table can be read only with administrator rights
options.D: The table's layout changes between versions

questions.explanation: Run with no arguments, `nvidia-smi` prints a table meant for people. A script should not parse it, because its layout changes between versions. The GPU probe instead asks for exactly the fields it wants with `--query-gpu` and `--format=csv,noheader,nounits`, which returns one comma-separated line per GPU. The table does show temperature and power, and it needs no administrator rights, so neither of those is the reason.

questions.chapter: Python Hardware Probes
questions.question_text: Why does the probe suite write a machine-readable report?

options.A: Later programs consume it, such as a model-fit calculator
options.B: It is shorter than the table that `nvidia-smi` prints
options.C: It can hold hostnames and serial numbers in a safely encoded form
options.D: It lets a probe change the settings of the machine that it reads

questions.explanation: A machine-readable report is output a program can parse without guessing, in contrast to text written for a person. The reason to produce one is that later steps consume it: a model-fit calculator reads `available_gib`, and a benchmark runner records the whole report beside each result so a number is never separated from the machine that produced it. The report deliberately contains no hostname, address, or account name.

questions.chapter: Python Hardware Probes
questions.question_text: A probe report shows `memory_total_mib: null` for the only GPU and `unified_memory: true`. Which figure should you use to judge whether a model fits?

options.A: The GPU's `power_w` reading from the same report
options.B: The storage probe's `free_gb` for the root filesystem
options.C: The RAM probe's `total_gib`, with nothing subtracted
options.D: The RAM probe's `available_gib`, less some headroom

questions.explanation: The unified memory probe is the check that the GPU's own memory fields are missing. When every GPU's total comes back as `None`, the probe sets `unified_memory` to true, and the figure to use is the system RAM probe's `available_gib`, minus the headroom Chapter 11 introduces. The `null` values are not an error; they are the unified-memory signature. Using `total_gib` would ignore what the operating system and other programs already hold.

questions.chapter: Python Hardware Probes
questions.question_text: You time a read of a model file that you loaded five minutes ago, and the measured speed is far higher than expected. What should you do?

options.A: Record the figure as the true read speed of the drive
options.B: Rerun on a file that has not been read since boot
options.C: Divide the result by the number of CPU cores
options.D: Rerun the same file with the GPU sitting idle

questions.explanation: A disk read benchmark reads an existing large file and divides the bytes by the seconds. The one trap is the operating system's page cache: a file read recently comes from memory, not the disk, so the number is far too high. The fix is to read a file that has not been touched since boot, such as a model file you have not loaded, and to say so in the report.

questions.chapter: Python Hardware Probes
questions.question_text: You are about to start a run that will last several hours on a unit that has stopped responding before. What should you start first?

options.A: A disk read benchmark on the largest model file
options.B: A vitals log that writes and syncs a line every 30 seconds
options.C: A probe verification test against a fake `meminfo` file
options.D: A full `nvidia-smi` table, saved once before the run

questions.explanation: Vitals logging records a few measurements at a fixed interval while a long job runs, so a machine that fails leaves its last readings behind. The loop writes one line every 30 seconds with available memory, GPU temperature, and power draw, and `flush` and `fsync` put each line on the disk at once, because a machine that freezes does not get to finish its buffers. A single snapshot taken before the run records nothing about the failure.

questions.chapter: Python Hardware Probes
questions.question_text: A probe returns 0 whenever it cannot read a value, and a report from a healthy machine shows `available_gib: 0`. What is wrong with this design?

options.A: Zero is not valid JSON, so the report cannot be parsed
options.B: The probe should keep retrying until the value becomes nonzero
options.C: A failed reading cannot be told apart from a measured zero
options.D: The probe should have read the value with `psutil`

questions.explanation: A probe script should report an unknown value as `null` and never guess. If a probe returns zero when it cannot read a value, a failed measurement looks like a machine with no memory, and the report appears complete while hiding the failure. Returning `null` lets a reader tell a missing measurement from a measured zero. Retrying without limit is no fix, because a probe must also have a bounded run time.

questions.chapter: Python Hardware Probes
questions.question_text: The suite runs on a machine with no GPU, where `nvidia-smi` is missing, yet the report still contains CPU, RAM, and storage results. Which design choices explain this?

options.A: The suite retries `nvidia-smi` until the GPU driver finally responds
options.B: The suite copies GPU values from the last saved report
options.C: The suite stops at the first error and prints whatever it has so far
options.D: Separate probes and a helper that returns `None` on failure

questions.explanation: A probe suite runs a set of probes together to produce one report. Every probe goes through a helper that returns `None` when a command is missing, fails, or times out, so a missing `nvidia-smi` gives an empty GPU answer instead of a crash. Keeping the probes separate and the suite thin means a single failing probe cannot take the others with it, and each probe can be tested alone.

questions.chapter: Model Sizing and Fit
questions.question_text: How is the memory for a model's weights calculated?

options.A: Parameter count times bytes per weight
options.B: Context length times KV bytes per token
options.C: Download size times the number of layers
options.D: Active parameters times bits per token

questions.explanation: Model weights are the learned numbers that make up a model, and loading a model means placing every one of them in memory. The memory they take is the parameter count times the size of one number, the bytes per weight. A 27-billion-parameter model needs 54 GB at 16-bit, 27 GB at 8-bit, and 13.5 GB at 4-bit. Context length times KV bytes per token gives the cache, a separate term in the estimate.

questions.chapter: Model Sizing and Fit
questions.question_text: What is the KV cache?

options.A: A disk folder where downloaded model files are stored
options.B: Memory holding key and value vectors for tokens in the context
options.C: The compute buffers and CUDA context the server allocates
options.D: A table of scaling factors stored inside a quantized file

questions.explanation: The KV cache is the memory a model uses to remember the conversation so far. For every token already in the context, the model keeps two vectors at every layer, the key and the value, so it does not recompute them for each new token. The cache grows by a fixed amount per token. Compute buffers and the CUDA context are runtime overhead, and scaling factors are part of a quantized file's overhead.

questions.chapter: Model Sizing and Fit
questions.question_text: What is safety headroom in a fit calculation, and what default does this course use?

options.A: Memory the server uses for compute buffers; 3 GB
options.B: Extra bits a quantized file stores per parameter; 5 bits
options.C: Memory reserved for the KV cache; 192 KiB per token
options.D: Memory deliberately left unused as a margin; 20%

questions.explanation: Safety headroom is memory deliberately left unused as a margin against what an estimate misses: the operating system, other processes, a cache that grows during a run, and an estimate that is simply low. It is expressed as a share of memory, and this course uses 20% as the default. On a unified-memory machine it is not a nicety, because exhausting a pool the operating system also runs on can freeze the whole machine.

questions.chapter: Model Sizing and Fit
questions.question_text: Why does a mixture-of-experts model not save memory compared with a dense model of similar total size?

options.A: Its experts are stored at a higher numeric precision
options.B: Its router keeps a second full copy of every expert's weights
options.C: Any expert may be chosen next, so all must stay in memory
options.D: Its KV cache grows with the number of experts that it holds

questions.explanation: A dense model uses all of its parameters for every token. A mixture-of-experts model routes each token to a small number of expert groups, so only its active parameters do the work. Memory is another matter: any expert may be chosen on the next token, so all parameters must be resident. The two Gemma models show it: similar total size and memory, and a threefold difference in speed. The design saves time per token, not memory.

questions.chapter: Model Sizing and Fit
questions.question_text: Why does a file labeled 4-bit measure nearer 5 bits per parameter?

options.A: It stores scaling factors and keeps some layers at higher precision
options.B: It bundles the whole KV cache needed for the model's full context length
options.C: It includes a second copy of the weights for error checking
options.D: It counts the tokenizer and license files as parameters

questions.explanation: A quantized file stores the scaling factors that let its small numbers be turned back into real ones, and it keeps some layers, often the most precision-sensitive, at higher precision. That extra is the quantized file overhead. The four "4-bit" files measured in this evaluation worked out to between 4.4 and 5.7 bits per parameter, so a planner using 4.0 would underestimate the weights by 10 to 30 percent and make the machine look roomier than it is.

questions.chapter: Model Sizing and Fit
questions.question_text: Why is a context-length setting described as a memory reservation?

options.A: The setting limits how many models the server can load
options.B: The cache is written to disk and then read back for each new token
options.C: The memory is claimed only once a conversation gets long
options.D: The cache is allocated at the full setting before any prompt

questions.explanation: Context length memory is the per-token KV cache amount times the number of tokens you allow. The cache is allocated for the context length the server is configured with, so it is reserved before the first prompt and cannot be ignored until a conversation gets long. This evaluation measured it: a 20 GB model took 29 GB at a 32,000-token setting and 66 to 71 GB at 256,000 tokens while idle. Choose the smallest context the job needs.

questions.chapter: Model Sizing and Fit
questions.question_text: A 48-billion-parameter model comes as a file labeled 4-bit. At the planned context its KV cache is 6.4 GB, and runtime overhead is 3 GB. Using 5.0 effective bits for the 4-bit file, how much memory does the model need?
questions.explanation: The memory estimation formula adds weights, KV cache, and overhead. Weights are parameters in billions times effective bits divided by 8, and a file labeled 4-bit uses 5.0 effective bits: 48 × 5.0 ÷ 8 = 30 GB. Adding the 6.4 GB cache and 3 GB of overhead gives 39.4 GB. Using exactly 4 bits gives 33.4 GB, which underestimates the weights, and 30 GB counts the weights alone.

questions.chapter: Model Sizing and Fit
questions.question_text: A model needs 110 GB on a 128 GB unified-memory machine, and the headroom is 20%. What is the verdict, and what should you do?

options.A: Fits; proceed with the run as planned
options.B: Does not fit; choose a smaller model or lower precision
options.C: Fits; raise the context length to use the spare memory
options.D: Fits without headroom; reduce context or use a smaller file

questions.explanation: A model-fit calculation compares memory needed with memory available after setting aside headroom. Usable memory is 128 × (1 − 0.20) = 102.4 GB. A need of 110 GB is above that and below 128 GB, which is the middle verdict, "Fits without headroom". The action is to reduce context or choose a smaller file, and not to run unattended. Such a model loads and then runs until something else asks for memory, which can be the operating system itself.

questions.chapter: Model Sizing and Fit
questions.question_text: A model needs 60 GB. Machine X has a 24 GB discrete GPU and 512 GB of system RAM. Machine Y has 128 GB of unified memory. On which machine does the model fit?

options.A: Only Y: the limit there is the shared pool, not a 24 GB GPU
options.B: Only X: its 512 GB of system RAM exceeds what is needed
options.C: Both: each machine has more than 60 GB of memory in total to draw on
options.D: Neither: 60 GB exceeds a 20% headroom on both machines

questions.explanation: Unified memory fit is the same calculation with the right number for memory. With dedicated GPU memory, the available memory is the GPU's free memory, so machine X's limit is 24 GB whatever its system RAM. On a unified-memory machine it is the system's available memory minus headroom: 128 GB × 0.80 is 102.4 GB, which holds a 60 GB need. The same model can fit on Y and not fit on X.

questions.chapter: Model Sizing and Fit
questions.question_text: The calculator returned "Fits" at 73.7 GB against a 102.4 GB limit, yet a unit stopped responding a few minutes into a long run at that setting. What does this show about the verdict?

options.A: The formula's arithmetic is wrong for large context settings
options.B: The 20% headroom should always be replaced by a 50% headroom
options.C: The estimate is a floor for the idle state, not a peak
options.D: The model's weights were really stored at 16 bits

questions.explanation: A fit verdict predicts the starting footprint. The 73.7 GB estimate matched the 71 GB measured with the model idle, so the arithmetic held. An estimate of the idle footprint is a floor, not a peak: the server's per-conversation state grows as a run proceeds. The cause of that freeze was not confirmed, so the lesson is limited: "Fits" means the idle state fits, not that a long run is safe, which is why a watchdog is added.

questions.chapter: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
questions.question_text: What does a model repository on the Hugging Face Hub hold?

options.A: A ranked table of models scored on shared tests
options.B: A versioned folder of weights, config, model card, and license
options.C: A cache directory on your machine for downloaded files
options.D: A credential that identifies your account to the hub

questions.explanation: The Hugging Face Hub is the main public site for sharing machine-learning models, and a model repository is one model's home on it: a versioned folder of files that holds the weights, the configuration, a README called the model card, and a license file. The repository page is a primary source, and reading it is the main selection skill. A ranked table of scores is a leaderboard, and a credential for the hub is an access token.

questions.chapter: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
questions.question_text: What does the Apache 2.0 license allow?

options.A: Use for research only, with commercial use forbidden
options.B: Use, modification, and redistribution, including commercial use
options.C: Use only by organizations below a revenue threshold
options.D: Use only after signing in and accepting the publisher's gating terms

questions.explanation: The Apache 2.0 license is a permissive open-source license. It allows use, modification, and redistribution, including commercial use, and it includes an express grant of patent rights from the contributors. It requires you to keep the license and copyright notices and to state changes, and it provides no warranty. For this evaluation it is the easy case: it raises no question about using a model's output in a published book.

questions.chapter: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
questions.question_text: Why should a leaderboard be used to build a long list and not to make the final decision?

options.A: Its tests rarely measure what your own workload demands
options.B: Its scores are computed only for closed models in the cloud
options.C: Its rankings change each time a listed model is downloaded
options.D: Its scores already include tool-calling reliability

questions.explanation: A model leaderboard ranks models by their scores on shared tests. Those scores are cheap evidence, and they answer a question that is rarely yours: a leaderboard of general knowledge or coding says little about whether a model follows a thousand-line skill file or keeps a blank line before every list. Use leaderboards to build a long list, and treat each published score as one more claim to check against what you measure.

questions.chapter: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
questions.question_text: Why does publisher provenance matter for an evaluation that will be published?

options.A: A repackaged file always takes more space on disk
options.B: Only the original publisher's files support tool calling
options.C: A recommendation is only as trustworthy as the file measured
options.D: A converted file cannot be verified with a checksum

questions.explanation: Publisher provenance answers the question "where did these weights actually come from?" A file with a famous model's name can be a conversion by a third party, a fine-tune, or something else. For an evaluation that will be published, your recommendation is only as trustworthy as the file it was measured on. Prefer the original publisher's repository, and when you use a conversion, say who made it.

questions.chapter: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
questions.question_text: What does a matching SHA-256 checksum tell you about a downloaded model file?

options.A: The file is the one the publisher released, unaltered and complete
options.B: The file's license permits commercial use of everything it generates
options.C: The file will fit in memory with the default headroom
options.D: The file is in the format the inference server expects

questions.explanation: A checksum is a fixed-length value computed from a file's bytes, and any change to the file changes the value. Checksum verification computes it for the file you received and compares it with the value the publisher states. A match means the file is the one the publisher released, unaltered and complete. A mismatch means a corrupt or substituted file, to be deleted and downloaded again. It says nothing about license terms or memory fit.

questions.chapter: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
questions.question_text: A candidate supports tool calling, has a 48,000-token context window, needs 22 GB of memory, and carries Apache 2.0 from an identified publisher. What is the decision for this course's workload?

options.A: Shortlist it, because it passes all four selection criteria
options.B: Exclude it, because it does not fit with headroom
options.C: Exclude it, because its license terms cannot be checked
options.D: Exclude it, because its window is under 64,000 tokens

questions.explanation: Model selection criteria come from the workload, not from a leaderboard. This course's workload needs tool calling, a context window of at least 64,000 tokens, a fit with headroom, and an identifiable publisher with checkable terms. This candidate passes three and fails the window test: 48,000 tokens is below the minimum, and the harness prompt alone takes about 19,000 tokens. A small memory footprint does not make up for a window that is too short.

questions.chapter: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
questions.question_text: You are about to pull a 65 GB model, and `df -h` shows 60 GB free. What should you do?

options.A: Start the pull, since downloads are compressed on disk
options.B: Start the pull inside `tmux` so it can finish overnight
options.C: Free space first, for example with `ollama rm <model>`
options.D: Pull the model in a second file format to save space

questions.explanation: Storage management is keeping the disk from filling. A download that runs out of space fails partway through and can leave a partial file behind, so a 65 GB model on a disk with 60 GB free fails after an hour. Check free space before a pull, and remove what you no longer need with the server's own command, such as `ollama rm <model>`. Running in `tmux` protects against a dropped session, not a full disk.

questions.chapter: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
questions.question_text: A gated model needs an access token, and a script will run the download. Where should the token be kept?

options.A: In the script, as a variable near the top of the file
options.B: In the repository's README, so collaborators can reuse it
options.C: In the run log, so the download can be reproduced later
options.D: In an environment variable or the tool's credential store

questions.explanation: A gated download needs an access token, a credential that identifies your account to the hub. Access token handling means treating it as a secret: keep it in an environment variable or the tool's credential store, not in a script. Never commit it, paste it into a chat, or let it appear in a log or a screenshot. Prefer a token limited to read access, and revoke it when the project ends.

questions.chapter: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
questions.question_text: One model was claimed to be fast, tested fastest, and still wrote a graph with 40 duplicate labels. Another claimed top tool-use scores and lost the task after a few steps. What do these results show about publisher claims?

options.A: Claims are false and should be ignored during selection
options.B: Claims are hypotheses to test against your own workload
options.C: Claims are reliable whenever they concern model speed
options.D: Claims remove the need for a model-only tool-calling test

questions.explanation: Publisher claims are statements a publisher makes about its model, and they are useful as hypotheses because they name the property the publisher optimized for. They do not state the conditions under which that property fails, and your workload may be one of them. One model was as fast as claimed and still produced duplicate labels; another claimed strong tool use and lost the task. A comparison therefore marks claims as claims and records what testing found.

questions.chapter: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
questions.question_text: The evaluation set aside its fastest model partly for broken navigation files, and the fault was later traced to a faulty example in the skill. What was the flaw in that exclusion?

options.A: The model was too large to fit with headroom on a single unit
options.B: The model's license had not been reviewed beforehand
options.C: The symptom's cause was unconfirmed and no retest was run
options.D: The model's download had not been checksum-verified

questions.explanation: An exclusion rationale is the reason a model was left off the shortlist. Here the navigation fault came from a faulty example in the skill, which the model had copied, and the model had not been retested. An exclusion based on a symptom needs the cause confirmed, and an exclusion that is not retested should say so in its rationale. Otherwise a model is dropped for a fault that was never its own.

questions.chapter: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
questions.question_text: What is an inference server?

options.A: A program that trains a model's parameters from data
options.B: A program that loads a model and answers generation requests
options.C: A public hub that hosts model repositories for download
options.D: A harness that runs an agent loop and executes its tools

questions.explanation: An inference server is a program that loads a trained model into memory and answers requests to generate text from it. It owns the hard parts of running a model: placing the weights on the GPU, managing the KV cache, scheduling requests, and turning raw output into text. Everything else in the stack talks to the server and never to the model directly. It does not train models, and the harness is a separate layer that calls it.

questions.chapter: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
questions.question_text: What does an OpenAI-compatible API let you do with a local server?

options.A: Send requests to the server without naming a model
options.B: Reach a localhost-bound server from any other machine you own
options.C: Download models from the server's library by their tags
options.D: Reuse OpenAI clients by changing only the base address

questions.explanation: The OpenAI-compatible API copies the request and response shapes of OpenAI's service, which became a de facto standard. A server that offers it can be called by any client written for that service, by changing only the base address. Its main route is the chat completions endpoint at `/v1/chat/completions`, which accepts a model name and a list of messages and returns the reply. Compatibility concerns the request format, not who can reach the server.

questions.chapter: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
questions.question_text: What happens by default to a loaded model after about five minutes without a request?

options.A: It is unloaded, and the next request pays the load time again
options.B: It is deleted from disk and must be pulled a second time before use
options.C: It moves from the GPU to the CPU in order to save power
options.D: It stays loaded until someone restarts the server

questions.explanation: Model keep-alive is how long an idle model stays loaded, set with `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE`. By default a model is unloaded after about five minutes without a request, which frees memory and means the next request pays the load time again. A benchmark that sends prompts minutes apart wants a longer keep-alive, and a machine that shares memory with other work may want a shorter one. Unloading removes the model from memory, not from disk.

questions.chapter: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
questions.question_text: What is the cost of a user-space installation of the server, compared with the usual system-wide installer?

options.A: The server cannot use the GPU without root access
options.B: The server is not a system service and will not start on its own
options.C: The server can load only models smaller than system RAM
options.D: The server must be reinstalled after each dropped SSH session ends

questions.explanation: A user-space installation unpacks a release archive into your own home directory, with no administrator rights and no system changes. The cost is that the server is not a system service and does not start on its own. The benefit is that removing it is deleting one directory. On a machine that belongs to someone else, a system-wide installer run with `sudo` is not a step to take on your own, so the trade is worth making.

questions.chapter: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
questions.question_text: Why is binding the server to `0.0.0.0` a security decision?

options.A: The endpoint has no login, so anyone who reaches it can use it
options.B: The setting disables the encryption on the tailnet's whole data plane
options.C: The setting sends each prompt to the model's publisher
options.D: The endpoint then demands administrator rights per request

questions.explanation: Localhost binding makes the server listen only on the loopback address `127.0.0.1`, so a request from any other machine is refused before it reaches the server. Binding to `0.0.0.0` accepts connections from any machine that can reach the port. That is a security decision because an inference endpoint has no login of its own: anyone who can send it a request can use the machine's GPU and read whatever the model is allowed to read.

questions.chapter: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
questions.question_text: What does running the server in a tmux session protect against, and what does it not?

options.A: It survives a dropped SSH connection but not a reboot
options.B: It survives a reboot but not a dropped SSH connection
options.C: It restarts the server automatically whenever it fails
options.D: It keeps other tailnet members from reaching the server

questions.explanation: A tmux session is a terminal that keeps running after you disconnect, so a server, a download, or a long benchmark continues when your SSH connection drops, and you can reattach later. It does not survive a reboot: after a restart the server is not running until someone starts it. Starting at boot and restarting after a failure are what a background service managed by the operating system provides.

questions.chapter: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
questions.question_text: Your first smoke-test request after a model was unloaded reports a very low tokens-per-second figure. What should you do before judging the model's speed?

options.A: Lower the context length and restart the server
options.B: Switch to a smaller quantization of the same model
options.C: Send the request again and read the second result
options.D: Rebind the server to all interfaces and then try again

questions.explanation: A first-prompt smoke test sends one tiny request and checks that the server answered, the reply is not empty, the speed is plausible, and the model is on the GPU. The first prompt after a model is unloaded pays for reading the file from disk, so its tokens per second looks terrible and is not the model's speed. Send it twice and read the speed from the second. If the second is also slow, look at the model, the context, or the memory.

questions.chapter: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
questions.question_text: On a unified-memory machine, `ollama ps` shows a loaded model at less than 100% on the GPU. What is the usual cause to check?

options.A: A keep-alive period that has been set too short
options.B: A context setting too large for weights and cache to fit
options.C: A server that is bound to the loopback address only
options.D: A model that was pulled from the Ollama model library

questions.explanation: GPU offload is placing the model's layers on the GPU, and on a unified-memory machine every layer is offloaded because the memory is shared. `ollama ps` shows what is loaded, how much memory it holds, and the share running on the GPU. A model below 100% is partly on the CPU and will be much slower. On a unified-memory machine that usually points to a context setting so large that the cache and weights no longer fit together.

questions.chapter: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
questions.question_text: A permitted member of the tailnet needs to reach a local endpoint, and the server must stay bound to the loopback address. Which method fits?

options.A: Bind the server to `0.0.0.0` so every interface listens
options.B: Forward a public port on the home router to the server
options.C: Hand the member your private SSH key for a port forward
options.D: Publish the port to the tailnet with Tailscale Serve

questions.explanation: Endpoint sharing makes a local endpoint reachable from other machines. Tailscale Serve publishes the loopback port to the tailnet over HTTPS while the server itself stays bound to the loopback address, and access is limited to tailnet members the access rules allow. Binding to `0.0.0.0` opens the port to anyone who can reach it, and a private key is never handed to another person. An SSH port forward reaches only the person who runs it.

questions.chapter: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
questions.question_text: A Python program on the DGX gets no usable reply from the endpoint, but the same request sent with `curl` from the same machine succeeds. What does this tell you?

options.A: The model is not loaded on the GPU
options.B: The server is bound to the wrong interface
options.C: The server and model work; the fault is in the client
options.D: The model's context window is too small for the prompt

questions.explanation: A `curl` request is the simplest way to call the endpoint: one command and no code. It removes every layer between you and the server, so a failure there is a failure of the server or the model and not of your program. Here `curl` succeeds from the same machine, so the server is running, the model answers, and the binding allows the request. What remains is the client program, such as its request body or how it reads the reply.

questions.chapter: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
questions.question_text: What does the Gemma 4 release offer that makes a clean comparison of two model designs?

options.A: A coding model and a general model released under the same license
options.B: Two dense models that differ only in context window
options.C: A cloud model and a local model with identical weights
options.D: A dense model and a mixture-of-experts model of similar size

questions.explanation: The Gemma family comes from Google and is offered in sizes that fit a single machine. Its Gemma 4 release includes both a dense model and a mixture-of-experts model at similar total size, which makes a clean comparison of the two designs. The two candidates here are `gemma4:31b`, the dense one, and `gemma4:26b`, the mixture-of-experts sibling. A general model alongside a coding model describes the Mistral family's pair instead.

questions.chapter: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
questions.question_text: How is IBM's Granite family positioned?

options.A: For always-on agents, with a one-million-token context window
options.B: For enterprise use, with a plain Apache 2.0 license
options.C: For coding agents, with a 384,000-token context window
options.D: For modest hardware, with strong results at a small size

questions.explanation: The Granite family comes from IBM. It is positioned for enterprise use, with a plain Apache 2.0 license, structured output, and documentation of its training data governance. Its one candidate here is `granite4.2:30b`, the conservative choice. Always-on agents and a one-million-token window describe NVIDIA's Nemotron candidate, and strong results at a size that fits modest hardware describe Microsoft's Phi family.

questions.chapter: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
questions.question_text: Why is none of the ten candidates a Phi model?

options.A: Phi models carry a license that forbids published use
options.B: The long skills and 64,000-token minimum favored larger models
options.C: Phi models cannot be served through the Ollama library
options.D: The Phi family has no model that supports tool calling

questions.explanation: The Phi family is Microsoft's line of small models, designed to give strong results at a size that fits modest hardware. None of the ten candidates is a Phi model because the benchmark's long skills and its 64,000-token minimum context favored larger models. That is a statement about this workload, not about the family's quality: a reader with less memory than this evaluation's unit would start with Phi.

questions.chapter: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
questions.question_text: Why could `gpt-oss:120b` run at a usable speed despite having 117 billion parameters?

options.A: Only about 5 billion of its parameters are active per token
options.B: Its weights are stored at 16 bits instead of 4 bits
options.C: It ran on both DGX units at once to share the load
options.D: Its context window was limited to 32,000 tokens

questions.explanation: `gpt-oss:120b` is a mixture-of-experts model. Only about 5 billion of its 117 billion parameters are active for each token, so it ran at 38 to 44 tokens per second and was the largest model that still ran at a usable speed. The dense `mistral-medium-3.5:128b`, which uses all of its parameters for every token, ran at 3 tokens per second. Storing weights at 16 bits would add memory and no speed.

questions.chapter: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
questions.question_text: Why did `qwen3.8:27b` take 102 minutes for the first stage when the five other models that finished took 6 to 22?

options.A: Its graph had 40 duplicate labels that had to be repaired by hand
options.B: It was stopped and restarted at the 150-minute limit
options.C: The server re-read almost the whole conversation each turn
options.D: Its download was the largest of the ten candidates

questions.explanation: `qwen3.8:27b` produced the cleanest learning graph of the first stage: exactly 200 concepts, no cycles, and no duplicate labels. It took 102 minutes where the five others that finished took 6 to 22, because the server re-read almost the whole conversation on every turn. The delay came from that repeated reading, not from a faulty graph, and in the later chapter-writing stage the model was too slow to finish a chapter inside 90 minutes.

questions.chapter: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
questions.question_text: You want a first-stage model that combines speed with a complete, correct result, judging only by the first round. Which candidate fits best?

options.A: `gemma4:26b`: under 6 minutes, with 40 duplicate labels
options.B: `qwen3.8:27b`: no structural fault, in 102 minutes
options.C: `granite4.2:30b`: stopped at the 150-minute limit
options.D: `qwen3.6:35b`: 22 minutes, with every file present

questions.explanation: `qwen3.6:35b` was the best combination of speed and correctness in the first round: 83 to 105 tokens per second and a learning graph in 22 minutes with every file present. Its graph is looser than the Qwen 3.8 one, with 19 concepts that have no prerequisite, but the faster `gemma4:26b` wrote 40 duplicate labels and the cleaner `qwen3.8:27b` needed 102 minutes. Each figure is a single run, so the choice is provisional.

questions.chapter: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
questions.question_text: You plan to use `gemma4:26b` for the learning-graph stage because it finishes in under six minutes. Given its first-round result, what should your pipeline add?

options.A: A longer time limit, since it ran out of time in that round
options.B: A larger context window, since its first prompt was too long
options.C: A check for duplicate labels that triggers a second attempt
options.D: A second unit, since the model does not fit on one machine

questions.explanation: `gemma4:26b` was the fastest model tested and finished the learning graph in under six minutes, but that graph has 40 duplicate concept labels out of 200, which is a serious flaw. A model this fast can afford a second attempt, but something has to notice that one is needed. A structural check for duplicate labels is that something. Time limits and memory were not its problem in the first round.

questions.chapter: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
questions.question_text: `granite4.2:30b` was stopped at the 150-minute limit in its single first-round run. Which statement may a report make?

options.A: In one run it reached the time limit with only a concept list
options.B: The model cannot produce a learning graph on this kind of hardware
options.C: The model is ranked last among the ten candidates tested
options.D: The Granite family is unsuitable for textbook generation

questions.explanation: Every first-round figure comes from a single attempt, so a result is a first observation, not a verdict. `granite4.2:30b` ran at 12 tokens per second and was stopped at the 150-minute limit having produced only the concept list, and a report may say exactly that. A model that failed once may succeed on a second try, so repeat a run before writing a sentence that begins "model X cannot". One run is not a ranking.

questions.chapter: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
questions.question_text: `muse-glimmer:30b` lost the task after a few steps in the harness. Which observation points to the likely cause?

options.A: It ran at only 3 tokens per second in the model-only smoke test
options.B: Its download was the largest of the ten candidates
options.C: Its first prompt took 35,000 tokens, far more than the others
options.D: It wrote 40 duplicate concept labels into its own learning graph

questions.explanation: `muse-glimmer:30b` lost the task after a few steps in the harness, which looks like a context problem: its first prompt took 35,000 tokens where the others took 17,000 to 21,000. That is a reading of the evidence, not a confirmed diagnosis. The other observations belong to different candidates: 3 tokens per second and the largest download were `mistral-medium-3.5:128b`, and the 40 duplicate labels were `gemma4:26b`.

questions.chapter: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
questions.question_text: What trade-off does the first round show between the dense `gemma4:31b` and its mixture-of-experts sibling `gemma4:26b`?

options.A: The dense model was faster, and the sibling followed rules better
options.B: The dense model needed far more memory for the same speed
options.C: Both ran at the same speed, and only their licenses differed
options.D: The dense model was slower but the more consistent rule-follower

questions.explanation: `gemma4:31b` is a dense model and was the most consistent rule-follower in the tests: it passed every model-only rule twice and ended every smoke run with a site that builds, at 28 to 40 tokens per second. Its mixture-of-experts sibling `gemma4:26b` was the fastest model tested, at 86 to 130 tokens per second, and wrote a graph with 40 duplicate labels. The pair trades speed against rule-following at a similar total size.

questions.chapter: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
questions.question_text: What does tokens per second measure?

options.A: How fast the server reads the tokens of the prompt
options.B: How long the server takes to load a model from disk
options.C: How many requests the server completes each second
options.D: How many output tokens the model produces each second

questions.explanation: Tokens per second is the generation speed: how many output tokens the model produces each second once it has started. Generation is slower than reading because each token depends on the one before it, so tokens are produced in sequence and each requires reading the model's active weights from memory. Reading the prompt has its own, much higher figure, the prompt processing speed. The measured generation speeds in this evaluation ranged from 3 to 130 tokens a second.

questions.chapter: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
questions.question_text: What is time to first token mostly made up of?

options.A: Model loading, if needed, and prompt processing
options.B: Generating the reply and running the requested tool
options.C: Sampling the next token at a high temperature
options.D: Writing the vitals log and checking the watchdog

questions.explanation: Time to first token is the delay between sending a request and receiving the first token of the reply. It is made up mostly of loading the model, if it is not already loaded, and prompt processing. One model in this evaluation read a 30,000-token prompt at about 3,000 tokens a second, so its time to first token was about ten seconds. Generating the rest of the reply and running tools come after the first token.

questions.chapter: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
questions.question_text: What does a temperature setting of 0 do?

options.A: It limits the choice to the k most likely tokens
options.B: It spreads the choice across less likely tokens
options.C: It always takes the most likely next token
options.D: It stops generation after the first token

questions.explanation: Sampling parameters control how the next token is chosen from the model's probabilities. Temperature scales how adventurous the choice is: 0 always takes the most likely token, and higher values spread the choice. Limiting the choice to the k most likely tokens is top-k, a different parameter. These settings change the output, so a benchmark must fix and record them, and they have little effect on speed.

questions.chapter: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
questions.question_text: How does prompt caching shorten an agent turn?

options.A: The server reuses saved state and reads only the new tokens
options.B: The harness stops resending the conversation after the first turn
options.C: The model writes several tokens of the reply in parallel
options.D: The server stores finished replies and returns them on later turns

questions.explanation: An agent harness resends the whole conversation on every turn. Prompt caching is the server's remedy: it keeps the already-computed internal state for the part of the prompt that has not changed, so each new turn only has to read what is new. With caching working, a turn that adds 2,000 tokens to a 50,000-token conversation reads 2,000. The harness still resends everything, and replies are still written one token at a time.

questions.chapter: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
questions.question_text: Why is latency, and not throughput, the figure that matters for a single benchmark session?

options.A: Throughput can be measured only on dedicated GPU memory
options.B: Throughput and latency are two names for the same figure
options.C: Only one request is in flight at a time, so latency governs
options.D: A benchmark session never generates more than one reply

questions.explanation: Latency is the total time for one request, from sending it to receiving the last token. Throughput is the total work done per unit of time across all requests in flight. For a single benchmark session only one request is in flight at a time, so latency is what you feel and throughput is irrelevant. For a service that generates many books at once, throughput is the number that sets the cost per book.

questions.chapter: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
questions.question_text: Why is thermal throttling invisible in a short speed test?

options.A: Throttling occurs only while the GPU is idle
options.B: Throttling is reported only in the model card
options.C: A short test reads the prompt but never writes a reply
options.D: A short test ends before the chassis has warmed up

questions.explanation: Thermal throttling is the chip reducing its own speed to stay below a safe temperature. It shows up as a speed that falls over a long run with no change in the workload. A thirty-second test finishes before the chassis has warmed, so the only way to find throttling is to run long and read temperature and tokens per second together. A speed that decays while the temperature climbs is the pattern to look for.

questions.chapter: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
questions.question_text: A server processes prompts at 500 tokens per second. Because of re-reading, each agent turn reads 55,000 tokens. How long does the reading take on each turn, before any reply token is written?

options.A: 11 seconds
options.B: 55 seconds
options.C: 110 seconds
options.D: 275 seconds

questions.explanation: Prompt processing speed is how fast the server reads the prompt, in input tokens per second. Reading time is the tokens read divided by that speed: 55,000 ÷ 500 is 110 seconds, before a single reply token is written. That is why a turn that re-reads most of a conversation is dominated by reading. With caching working, the same turn would read only the new tokens, perhaps 2,000, in about four seconds at this speed.

questions.chapter: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
questions.question_text: Two runs differ in quantization, context length, and keep-alive, and the second is faster. What should you do to learn which setting mattered?

options.A: Average the two runs and report the mean speed
options.B: Change one setting at a time against a fixed baseline
options.C: Keep all three changes, since the second run was faster
options.D: Raise the temperature and see whether the speed changes

questions.explanation: Performance optimization is changing one setting at a time and measuring the result against a fixed baseline: one change, one measurement, then restore. A comparison between two runs that differ in three settings tells you nothing about which one mattered. Each setting moves a different part of the time, so the single-change discipline is also how you confirm that the setting aimed at your bottleneck is the one that helped.

questions.chapter: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
questions.question_text: A vitals log shows available memory falling from 72 GiB at the start of a run to 18 GiB near the end, and the job has slowed. What is the condition, and which figure does a watchdog act on?

options.A: Memory pressure; the watchdog acts on the low, later figure
options.B: Thermal throttling; the watchdog acts on the starting figure
options.C: Prompt re-reading; the watchdog acts on tokens read per turn
options.D: A model reload; the watchdog acts on the keep-alive period

questions.explanation: Memory pressure is the condition in which available memory is low enough that the system starts to struggle: it swaps, stalls, or kills a process. It builds gradually as the context grows, and the symptom is a job that slows for no obvious reason late in a run. The vitals log records available memory every 30 seconds, so the slope is visible. A fall from 72 GiB to 18 GiB is growing pressure, and the second number is the one a watchdog acts on.

questions.chapter: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
questions.question_text: In a turn with prompt re-reading, reading takes 110 of the 138 seconds. What would tripling the generation speed do to that turn?

options.A: The turn would take about a third as long
options.B: The turn would barely change, since reading dominates
options.C: The turn would get slower, since the tool would then wait
options.D: The turn would fail, since the KV cache would overflow

questions.explanation: A turn's time is reading plus writing plus tool time. With prompt re-reading, the server recomputes most of the conversation on each turn, so the first term dominates: 55,000 tokens at 500 per second is 110 of the 138 seconds. Tripling the generation speed would shorten only the 23 seconds of writing, so the turn would barely change. The setting to fix first is the one aimed at the bottleneck, which here is caching.

questions.chapter: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
questions.question_text: What does an AI agent harness supply that the model does not?

options.A: The language ability that produces each next message in turn
options.B: The trained weights that are loaded onto the GPU
options.C: The GPU memory that holds the conversation's cache
options.D: The tools, permission rules, and loop around the model

questions.explanation: An AI agent harness is the program that wraps a language model so it can act in the world. The model supplies language: given a conversation, it produces the next message. The harness supplies everything else: the system prompt that sets the task, the list of tools, the code that carries out tool calls, the rules that allow or refuse them, and the bookkeeping that keeps the conversation going. Because it is separate software, the model underneath can be swapped.

questions.chapter: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
questions.question_text: When does the agent loop end?

options.A: When the context window is completely full
options.B: When the harness has run a fixed number of turns
options.C: When a tool returns a result that has no errors
options.D: When the model's reply contains no tool call

questions.explanation: The agent loop sends the conversation to the model. If the reply contains a request to call a tool, the harness runs the tool, appends the result, and sends the conversation again. If the reply contains no tool call, the loop ends and the reply is the final answer. That rule has a sharp edge: a model that writes a tool call as plain text ends the run early, because the harness sees no tool call.

questions.chapter: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
questions.question_text: Why does the prompt for turn 40 of an agent session contain everything from turns 1 to 39?

options.A: Each turn appends its reply and tool result to the conversation
options.B: The model stores earlier turns in its parameters between requests
options.C: The server merges all open sessions into a single prompt
options.D: The harness resends only the system prompt on each turn

questions.explanation: An agent turn is one trip around the loop: one request to the model and one response, plus the tool call and result if there was one. Each turn appends a reply and a result, so the conversation only grows, and the prompt of turn 40 contains everything in turns 1 to 39. The model keeps nothing between requests. Every turn is a full request with everything so far, which is why prompt caching matters so much.

questions.chapter: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
questions.question_text: Why might a local model that struggles in the harness be struggling with the system prompt and not with the task?

options.A: The system prompt changes on every turn of the loop
options.B: It runs to about 19,000 tokens and was written for Claude models
options.C: The system prompt is sent only once, on the first turn
options.D: It is truncated by the harness before the model reads it

questions.explanation: The system prompt is the standing instruction that opens every conversation. In a harness it is long, and it is resent at the start of every turn unchanged, which is what makes it cacheable. Claude Code's own instructions and tool definitions run to about 19,000 tokens, and they were written for Claude models. A local model may be struggling with that prompt and not with the task, which is one reason a model is tested alone first.

questions.chapter: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
questions.question_text: How does context compaction differ from context truncation?

options.A: Compaction drops the oldest content; truncation summarizes it
options.B: Compaction raises the server's window; truncation lowers it
options.C: Compaction summarizes earlier content; truncation drops the oldest
options.D: Compaction removes the tool definitions; truncation removes the replies

questions.explanation: When a conversation approaches the window, a harness can shrink it in two ways. Context truncation drops the oldest content, which is crude: the beginning of the conversation, which holds the task, is exactly what disappears. Context compaction asks the model to summarize the earlier conversation into a short note and replaces the old content with it. Compaction keeps the thread and loses detail, and it costs a model call.

questions.chapter: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
questions.question_text: You are preparing an unattended overnight run of a skill that asks approval questions. What must you do beforehand?

options.A: Leave the approval rules on and check how the run went in the morning
options.B: Settle every approval in advance and confirm with a short test
options.C: Remove the shell execution tool so nothing needs approval
options.D: Raise the context window so the questions fit in the prompt

questions.explanation: The permission model is the set of rules that allow a tool call, forbid it, or require a person to approve it first. An unattended run has nobody to ask, so an approval rule stalls it and it produces nothing. Decide every approval in advance, either by allowing the call or by putting a standing answer in the prompt, and confirm with a short test run that nothing pauses. Removing the shell tool is no answer, because most skills need it.

questions.chapter: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
questions.question_text: A tool definition for `read_file` lists `path` under `required` in its `input_schema`. A model emits a structured request to `read_file` with no `path`. What is this request?

options.A: A valid call, because the tool name matches the definition
options.B: A malformed call, because a required argument is missing
options.C: A final answer, because it contains no structured request
options.D: A permission error, because reading files needs approval

questions.explanation: A tool definition gives the model a tool's name, a description of when to use it, and an `input_schema` listing the arguments and their types, so the harness can check a request before running it. The `read_file` definition marks `path` as required. A request with a missing argument or a wrong name is a malformed tool call. A matching name is not enough, and a structured request is not a final answer.

questions.chapter: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
questions.question_text: Two models peaked at 135,000 and 147,000 tokens of context in one stage. You plan to rerun that stage with a 128,000-token window. What should you expect?

options.A: Both runs would be cut off, since their peaks exceed the window
options.B: Both runs would fit, since peak context is measured in words
options.C: Both runs would fit, since only the first prompt must fit
options.D: The harness would enlarge the server's window as needed

questions.explanation: Peak context size is the largest the conversation reached in a run, and it tells you whether a window was big enough. Context management must keep the conversation within the window, which is a fixed limit measured in tokens. Peaks of 135,000 and 147,000 tokens both exceed 128,000, so a window of that size would have cut both runs off. The harness cannot enlarge the server's window; that is a server setting with a memory cost.

questions.chapter: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
questions.question_text: Claude Code assumes a window of about 200,000 tokens, but the server is configured with a smaller one. What goes wrong?

options.A: The harness compacts too early and wastes model calls
options.B: The server rejects every request with an explicit error message
options.C: The model's tool definitions are dropped from each of its replies
options.D: The server truncates silently before the harness compacts

questions.explanation: Truncation and compaction interact dangerously with the server's window. Claude Code assumes a window of about 200,000 tokens, so it does not compact until the conversation nears that size. If the server was configured with a smaller window, the server truncates silently before the harness knows to compact, and the model loses the start of its own task without any message. This is why the evaluation raised the server's context setting, at a memory cost.

questions.chapter: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
questions.question_text: Why must the orchestrator in this evaluation never write benchmark content?

options.A: The orchestrator has no file editing tool available to it
options.B: The orchestrator runs inside the container on the DGX
options.C: It uses a cloud model, and the test is of a local one
options.D: It lacks the context window needed to hold a full chapter

questions.explanation: An orchestrator starts work and coordinates it without doing it. In this evaluation it is a Claude Code session using a cloud model on the laptop, which starts runs, watches them, and scores results. The harness on the DGX generates, by calling the local model. Role separation keeps these distinct: the orchestrator never writes benchmark content, because the question is whether a local model can. Content written by the cloud model would answer a different question.

questions.chapter: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
questions.question_text: What is an agent skill?

options.A: A folder of instructions that teaches a harness one kind of task
options.B: A new tool that adds a capability the harness lacked
options.C: A fine-tuned model that replaces the default model inside the harness
options.D: A log of the tool calls made during a finished run

questions.explanation: An agent skill is a folder of instructions, and sometimes helper files, that teaches a harness how to carry out one kind of task well. It is a procedure written down so a model can follow it: the steps, the order, the checks, and the formats of the files to produce. A skill does not add a capability the harness lacks. It supplies knowledge of how to use the capabilities it has, which makes results repeatable.

questions.chapter: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
questions.question_text: Which steps of the ten-step `ibook-skills` chain does the benchmark run as its stages?

options.A: All ten, from the course description to the installer
options.B: Three: the learning graph, chapter structure, and chapter content
options.C: Two: the glossary and the chapter quizzes
options.D: Five: every step up to and including the MicroSims

questions.explanation: The `ibook-skills` skill chain is the ordered set of ten skills that builds an intelligent textbook, each taking the previous one's output as its input. This benchmark runs three of the ten, steps 2 through 4: the learning graph, the chapter structure, and the chapter content. Step 1, the course-description analyzer, serves as a short check that the wiring works. MicroSims, the glossary, the FAQ, and the quizzes are outside the benchmark.

questions.chapter: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
questions.question_text: Which two header fields of a `SKILL.md` file identify a skill and let a harness decide when it applies?

options.A: `name` and `description`
options.B: `license` and `metadata`
options.C: `scripts` and `assets`
options.D: `title` and `summary`

questions.explanation: The `SKILL.md` format is a Markdown file that opens with a block of YAML metadata, followed by the procedure. Two fields do the work. The `name` is the identifier and matches the directory name. The `description` is the text the harness uses to decide when the skill is relevant, so it must say both what the skill does and when to use it. A skill with an unclear description is invisible, however good its body is.

questions.chapter: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
questions.question_text: Why does a harness load skills in stages?

options.A: So each skill can be edited by the model between its loading stages
options.B: So the model can run scripts before reading the header
options.C: So skills from different harnesses do not overwrite each other
options.D: So context is not spent on instructions that are not needed

questions.explanation: Skill loading works in stages so that context is not spent on instructions that are not needed. At startup the harness reads only each installed skill's name and description and places those short entries in the system prompt. It loads a skill's `SKILL.md` body when that skill is selected, and reference documents later still, one at a time, when a step names them. A harness with thirty skills cannot read thirty full procedures on every request.

questions.chapter: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
questions.question_text: Why are the skills mounted read-only inside the benchmark container?

options.A: So the skills load faster at the start of every turn
options.B: So a model cannot alter the test it is being measured against
options.C: So the container can start up without any access to the network
options.D: So the harness skips the skill descriptions at startup

questions.explanation: Skill installation places the skill directories where the harness looks for them. Inside the benchmark container the skills are mounted read-only, marked by the `:ro` suffix, so the agent can read every skill and cannot change any of them. That matters for the comparison: a model that rewrote a skill to make its own task easier would be measuring itself against a different test than the other models faced.

questions.chapter: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
questions.question_text: Why was Claude Code chosen as the harness for this evaluation?

options.A: It has the lightest system prompt of the harnesses compared
options.B: It is the only harness that implements the skill format
options.C: It can reach Anthropic's service when a local model fails
options.D: The comparison books and the skills were made with it

questions.explanation: Claude Code is Anthropic's command-line coding agent and the harness this evaluation uses. It was chosen for a practical reason: the published comparison books were generated with it and the skills were written for it, so using it makes the model the only thing that changes. Its prompt is not the lightest; OpenCode's is lighter. It is also given a placeholder credential, so it cannot reach Anthropic's service even if it tried.

questions.chapter: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
questions.question_text: You are configuring Claude Code to use a model served by a local endpoint. Which settings point it at the local server without a real credential?

options.A: `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` to the local endpoint, with a placeholder token
options.B: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` to a real key, with the vendor's default base address
options.C: `API_TIMEOUT_MS` to zero, with the vendor's address unchanged
options.D: `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` to a cloud model name, with no base address

questions.explanation: A local endpoint connection points the harness at your own server through environment variables. `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` is the address requests go to, here the local endpoint. `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` is a placeholder word, which is enough because the local server does not check it, and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is left empty so no real key is used. The model variables are all set to the same local model's tag, so the harness never asks for a name that does not exist.

questions.chapter: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
questions.question_text: A three-minute run of the course-description analyzer has finished. Which set of checks tells you the skill executed correctly?

options.A: The server answered, and the reply was not empty
options.B: The run log exists, and the run used fewer than 150 turns
options.C: Report written, score given, files updated, strict build passes
options.D: The model loaded on the GPU, and its speed was plausible

questions.explanation: Skill execution verification confirms that a skill ran to completion and produced what it should. It tests the harness, the model, and the skill together. The short analyzer run passes when four things are true: the report was written, a quality score was given, the frontmatter and navigation were updated, and a strict `mkdocs build` finishes with no errors. An answering server and a plausible speed belong to the first-prompt smoke test, which tests only the server.

questions.chapter: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
questions.question_text: You want a headless stage run that records every message, tool call, and result as a line of JSON. Which flags of the `claude` command do that?

options.A: `--max-turns 150` with `--model <model>`
options.B: `--dangerously-skip-permissions` by itself
options.C: `-p` with `--output-format stream-json --verbose`
options.D: `--verbose` with the prompt typed into an interactive session

questions.explanation: Harness configuration is the environment variables plus the command-line flags. `-p` runs Claude Code non-interactively, and `--output-format stream-json --verbose` writes each message, tool call, and result as a line of JSON, which is the record later chapters analyze. `--max-turns` only caps the loop so a confused model cannot run forever, and `--dangerously-skip-permissions` removes approval prompts, which is acceptable only inside the sandbox.

questions.chapter: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
questions.question_text: A model passes the first-prompt smoke test and then fails the three-minute skill run by writing its tool call as plain text. What does this pattern show?

options.A: The smoke test was run with the wrong context length on the server
options.B: The skill's description did not say when to use it
options.C: The server lost the model between the two tests
options.D: The smoke test covers only the server, not harness tool use

questions.explanation: A harness compatibility test runs the same short skill against several harness and model combinations to find which pairs work at all. The first-prompt smoke test checks only the server: that it answers and how fast. It does not exercise tool calls through the harness. In this evaluation the short skill run exposed a model that wrote its first tool call as plain text within minutes, a failure that a first-prompt smoke test would not have found.

questions.chapter: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
questions.question_text: What is a Docker container?

options.A: An isolated process with its own view of the filesystem
options.B: A full virtual machine with its own operating system kernel
options.C: A background service that starts the model server at boot
options.D: A firewall rule that limits where a process can connect

questions.explanation: Docker runs programs in containers. A container is an isolated process with its own view of the filesystem, built from an image, a packaged set of files and settings. It shares the host's operating system kernel and is not a full virtual machine, so it starts in a second and costs little. The isolation is real and it is partial, and what it covers depends on how the container is started.

questions.chapter: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
questions.question_text: Inside the harness container, what may the agent do, and where can it write?

options.A: Run only pre-approved commands, and write anywhere on the host
options.B: Run no shell commands, and write only to the skills folder
options.C: Run any command as root, and write to the host's home directory
options.D: Run any command, and write only to deliberately mounted paths

questions.explanation: The harness container holds the agent, and the container sandbox is the boundary it creates: inside it the agent may run any command, and the only paths it can write to are the ones deliberately mounted in. The run directory is mounted writable, the harness's own state folder is separate, and the skills are read-only. The image also uses a non-root user, so the agent cannot do what only root can do, even inside its own container.

questions.chapter: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
questions.question_text: Why was adding the benchmark account to the `docker` group a decision for the Administrator?

options.A: Group members can change the tailnet's access control list directly
options.B: The group gives a user ownership of the model files
options.C: A member can mount any host directory, like an administrator
options.D: The group is required before a user can log in over SSH

questions.explanation: Docker group membership is the permission that lets a user run `docker` commands. Because the Docker service runs as `root`, a member of the group can start a container that mounts any directory of the host, which makes membership equivalent to administrator access. That is why the Administrator, and not the evaluator, decided it. Until the account was added, every Docker command failed with `permission denied`.

questions.chapter: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
questions.question_text: Why was the harness container started with `--network host`?

options.A: So the agent could download packages while it runs
options.B: So it could reach the server on the host's loopback address
options.C: So the container would be isolated from the tailnet
options.D: So the GPU would be visible inside the container

questions.explanation: Host network mode, set with `--network host`, makes a container share the host's network instead of having its own. The harness container was started this way so it could reach the model server, which listens only on the host's loopback address; a container on its own network cannot see the host's loopback. The harness container does not need the GPU at all, because the model runs in the server on the host.

questions.chapter: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
questions.question_text: Why would a claim that "everything stayed local" be false for this evaluation?

options.A: The harness sent every prompt to the vendor's service
options.B: The cloud orchestrator read output to monitor and score runs
options.C: The model server uploaded its weights after each stage
options.D: The coordination service stored a copy of each generated chapter

questions.explanation: Supervision data exposure is the data that reaches a third party because something is watching the run, even though the run itself is local. Here the orchestrator is a cloud model, and everything it reads back to monitor or score a run, including generated text and log excerpts, goes to its service. The generation loop kept its tokens local, and the supervision of it did not. That is not a flaw in the setup, but it has to be stated.

questions.chapter: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
questions.question_text: After a run, the files in the run directory are owned by a different user, and you need elevated rights to delete them. What should you change?

options.A: Start the container without the `--network host` option
options.B: Mount the skills folder without the `:ro` suffix
options.C: Build the image with your own `UID` and `GID` arguments
options.D: Add `--rm` so the container is deleted when it ends

questions.explanation: A non-root container user has ordinary permissions inside the container and is created in the image with the same numeric user and group identifiers as the account that started the run. Files the agent writes then belong to the evaluator and not to `root`, so they can be read and deleted without special rights. Build the image with your own identifiers, using the `UID` and `GID` build arguments, or cleanup needs elevated rights.

questions.chapter: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
questions.question_text: You have no administrator rights but want a basic check of where a running harness connects. What can you do?

options.A: Run a full packet capture on the network interface
options.B: List established connections with `ss` and check each peer
options.C: Read the model card for a list of contacted hosts
options.D: Set a placeholder credential and assume nothing leaves

questions.explanation: Packet capture verification watches the network interface during a run and confirms that the only traffic is what the trace says, but reading raw packets needs administrator rights. A lighter check needs none and catches the gross cases: while a run is going, list the established connections with `ss -tnH state established` and look for any peer that is not the loopback address. A placeholder credential is configuration, not verification, and an unverified boundary is a hypothesis.

questions.chapter: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
questions.question_text: You are writing the egress trace for a local-generation setup in which a script uploads each generated chapter to a cloud scoring service. Where does this flow belong?

options.A: Nowhere, because the model itself runs locally
options.B: Under loopback traffic, because the script itself runs on the DGX
options.C: In the trace, as a third-party destination with what is sent
options.D: Under one-time downloads, because uploads are counted only once

questions.explanation: A data egress trace is an accounting of every place a system's data goes when it leaves, built component by component with the destination, what is sent, and how often. Whatever reads the output, whether a reviewer, a scoring script that uploads, or a supervising assistant, can send it away. The upload therefore gets its own row as a third-party destination. "The model runs locally" is not the same claim as "nothing leaves".

questions.chapter: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
questions.question_text: The harness container limits the agent's writes to the run directory, yet it is described as not being a network sandbox. What explains the difference?

options.A: Mounts bound the filesystem; host networking shares the host's reach
options.B: The non-root user is allowed to change the host's firewall rules
options.C: The read-only skills mount exposes the tailnet to the agent
options.D: The placeholder credential opens the vendor's service to the agent's calls

questions.explanation: The mounts decide what files the agent can reach, so the container is a real filesystem sandbox. Host network mode is a separate setting: a container that shares the host's network can reach anything the host can, including the internet, other machines on the tailnet, and every service on the host's loopback. That is the network sandbox gap. The agent can be told not to reach out, and a model that has been told is not a boundary.

questions.chapter: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
questions.question_text: One unit stopped responding twice. The second time, a watchdog was running at a smaller context and logged no action. What does this evidence support?

options.A: The freeze was caused by the 256,000-token context setting
