options.B: The watchdog itself caused the machine to stop responding
options.C: The model's weights were corrupted during the download
options.D: Memory exhaustion as the sole cause is not confirmed

questions.explanation: A system freeze is the machine ceasing to respond entirely, which needs the Administrator to restart it. The first freeze was at a 256,000-token context. The second was at a smaller context with a watchdog running, and the watchdog logged no action, so memory exhaustion as the only cause is not confirmed. Heat, power, and the memory hardware itself were not ruled out. A watchdog guards against the failure you expect; it is not a diagnosis of the one you get.

questions.chapter: Designing a Fair Evaluation
questions.question_text: What are controlled variables?

options.A: The outcomes that are recorded in the same way for each and every run
options.B: The factors that changed without anyone deciding they should
options.C: The factors that could affect the result, held fixed on purpose
options.D: The single factor that the experiment deliberately changes

questions.explanation: Controlled variables are everything other than the independent variable that could affect the result, which the design holds fixed on purpose. They are the reason a difference can be blamed on the independent variable. In this evaluation they include the course, the prompts, the harness and server versions, the skills, the hardware, and the quantization. Each one is a written decision, and a factor that varied without being decided is an uncontrolled variable.

questions.chapter: Designing a Fair Evaluation
questions.question_text: What are fixed inputs?

options.A: The exact files and prompts that every run starts from
options.B: The metrics chosen after the first results are seen
options.C: The hardware settings that differ from one model to the next
options.D: The logs that each run writes while it is still in progress

questions.explanation: Fixed inputs are the exact files and prompts every run starts from. They are the most concrete controlled variable and the cheapest to get right. Here the course description is an unchanged copy, the starting workspace is copied fresh for every run, and each stage has one prompt file. Keep them in version control so a change is visible, and copy them into each run so that no run can alter the input of the next.

questions.chapter: Designing a Fair Evaluation
questions.question_text: Why must metrics be chosen before the data is seen?

options.A: Metrics chosen later cannot be computed by a program
options.B: Completion metrics are available only before a run starts
options.C: The server discards token counts once a run has ended
options.D: Choosing afterward lets you pick what flatters a favorite

questions.explanation: Metric selection is choosing what to measure, and a metric is useful only if it answers the question, can be computed the same way for every run, and was decided before you saw the data. If you look at the data and then choose the measure that makes your favorite model look best, you have not run an experiment. Write the metrics into the record before the first run, and add new ones later only as clearly labeled extras.

questions.chapter: Designing a Fair Evaluation
questions.question_text: What is the purpose of a control run?

options.A: To give a slow model a second chance to finish its stage in time
options.B: To check the apparatus by repeating a run that should match
options.C: To compare a local model's output with a cloud model's
options.D: To measure how a model behaves with its reasoning mode turned off

questions.explanation: A control run is a repeat of a run that should give the same answer, done to check the apparatus and not the subject. If the control differs from the original by more than the expected variation, something in the setup changed in between, such as memory pressure, a thermal state, or a server setting. It is cheap, and it separates "this model really behaves this way" from "this machine behaved differently this afternoon".

questions.chapter: Designing a Fair Evaluation
questions.question_text: A team proposes the evaluation question "Is our new model good?" Which revision makes it a question an experiment can answer?

options.A: "Is our new model really good across the tasks that matter to us?"
options.B: "Does it finish stage 1 with no structural faults within 150 minutes?"
options.C: "Is our new model better than most people would expect it to be?"
options.D: "Does our new model work well on the machine we already own?"

questions.explanation: An evaluation question is the single, answerable question the experiment exists to answer. A good one names what is being compared, on what task, under what conditions, and what would count as an answer. The test is whether you can imagine two different outcomes. Only the revision with a named stage, a structural-fault criterion, and a time limit can come out "yes" or "no". The others still leave "good", "better", and "well" undefined.

questions.chapter: Designing a Fair Evaluation
questions.question_text: You have ten new candidate models and limited time. Following two-layer testing, what do you run first?

options.A: Short fixed tasks sent to the server, with no harness
options.B: The full three-stage pipeline, run for each model in turn
options.C: The three-minute skill run through the harness
options.D: A cloud baseline run of all three benchmark stages

questions.explanation: Two-layer testing tests a model alone first and then inside the harness. The model-only test sends short, fixed tasks directly through the server, with no harness, and checks the output against rules. It takes minutes, and a failure there has a cause you can name. Going straight to the full pipeline makes every failure slow and mixes the causes. The three-minute harness smoke test is the second layer, for the models that pass the first.

questions.chapter: Designing a Fair Evaluation
questions.question_text: The model-only tests ran with reasoning turned off, and the harness runs used each model's own default. One model then spent nineteen minutes on a single turn. What role does reasoning mode play in this design?

options.A: An uncontrolled variable that is mixed with the model itself
options.B: The independent variable that the design deliberately set out to change
options.C: A controlled variable, since each model used its default
options.D: A measured result that is recorded for every run

questions.explanation: An uncontrolled variable is something that could affect the result and that the design did not hold fixed. Reasoning mode was off in the model-only tests and left at each model's own default in the harness runs, so it differed by model without being decided. It is therefore mixed with the independent variable, and predictions from the model-only test did not match the harness runs. Using each model's default is not control; control is a deliberate, recorded choice.

questions.chapter: Designing a Fair Evaluation
questions.question_text: Model X finishes a stage in 20 minutes on one run and 45 on another. Model Y finishes in 30 minutes on its only run. What can be concluded about which model is faster?

options.A: X is faster, because its best run beat Y's run
options.B: Y is faster, because it beat X's average of 32.5 minutes
options.C: They are equal, because the three run times average out evenly
options.D: Neither claim holds; X's spread spans Y's single result

questions.explanation: Run variance is how much results differ among repeated runs of the same configuration. A single run is a sample of one and supports a statement about that run only. X's two runs span 20 to 45 minutes, and Y's single 30-minute run falls inside that spread, so ranking either ahead of the other is a coin flip. With five runs of each, the spread is visible and the comparison can be stated with its uncertainty.

questions.chapter: Designing a Fair Evaluation
questions.question_text: Why is the published Algebra I book a reference for scale and not yet a baseline for the local runs?

options.A: It used a different course description from the local runs
options.B: It used earlier skill versions and kept no timings or token counts
options.C: It was written by a local model on a different DGX unit
options.D: It has fewer concepts and chapters than the local runs produced

questions.explanation: A baseline comparison judges a result against a reference produced under the same rules. The published Algebra I book used the same course description, but it was made with earlier versions of the skills, its prompts were not recorded, and no timings or token counts were kept. It shows how large a finished book is. It cannot say how long a cloud model takes or how good its output is under these conditions, so the cloud baseline remains to be run.

questions.chapter: Designing a Fair Evaluation
questions.question_text: Three designs are proposed for comparing ten models. Design 1 changes only the model. Design 2 also lets each model use its own best context length and reasoning setting. Design 3 splits the models across two DGX units. Which design best answers "which model performs best on this task", and why?

options.A: Design 2, because each model is shown at its tuned best
options.B: Design 3, because two units finish the runs in half the time
options.C: Design 1, because any difference can be blamed on the model
options.D: Design 2, because more settings give more data per run

questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one thing the experiment deliberately changes, and the discipline is to change one thing. Design 1 varies only the model, so a difference in results can be attributed to it. Design 2 varies three things together, and design 3 mixes the model with the machine, so neither can say why runs differ. Design 2 may be worth running as a separate experiment about tuning, but not presented as a comparison of models.

questions.chapter: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
questions.question_text: What is a scoring rubric?

options.A: A script that checks whether an output file parses
options.B: A single number computed from all automated checks
options.C: A written description of what earns each score
options.D: A list of the models ranked by first-round results

questions.explanation: A scoring rubric is a written description of what a result must have to earn each score. It makes a judgment repeatable: two reviewers using the same rubric on the same chapter should give scores that are close. A rubric needs dimensions, a scale, and a description of each level. Without one, "good" means whatever the reviewer felt that day. A single computed number is an automated quality score, which hides the per-dimension profile.

questions.chapter: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
questions.question_text: Why does passing every structural check not mean a learning graph is good?

options.A: Structural checks are too slow to run on a whole graph
options.B: The checks test form, so the concepts may still be wrong ones
options.C: Structural checks can be run only by a human reviewer
options.D: The checks pass any graph that has exactly 200 concepts

questions.explanation: Structural checks are the checks a program can run on the form of the output without judging its meaning: does the file exist, does it parse, does it agree with its twin. They are cheap, repeatable, and fast. A structural pass does not mean the content is good: a learning graph can have no cycles and no duplicates and still be a graph of the wrong concepts. The checks are a gate, and the grade is a separate matter.

questions.chapter: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
questions.question_text: Why should a report state what did not work with the same care as what did?

options.A: Failures are rare, so listing them costs a report very little space
options.B: A failure is data that readers need and others would repeat
options.C: Negative results raise a report's automated quality score
options.D: Failures prove that local models cannot generate usable textbooks

questions.explanation: Negative result reporting is stating what did not work, and why, with the same care as what did. A failure is data: a model that lost the task, one that wrote its tool call as plain text, and one that could not fit a usable context are all findings, and a reader choosing a model needs them. Omitting them makes a field look easier than it is and makes the next person repeat them.

questions.chapter: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
questions.question_text: In a generated graph, concept X has no prerequisites, and three other concepts depend on it. Concept Y has no prerequisites and no dependents. How should each be classified?

options.A: Both are orphans, because neither has a prerequisite
options.B: X is an orphan, and Y is a foundational concept
options.C: X is foundational, and Y is an orphan
options.D: Both are foundational, because neither has a prerequisite

questions.explanation: Orphaned concepts have no prerequisite and no dependent, so they are connected to nothing and cannot be reached from the rest of the graph. They are different from foundational concepts, which have no prerequisites and do have dependents. X has three dependents, so it is foundational and not a defect. Y is connected to nothing, so it is an orphan. Flagging every concept without a prerequisite would mark the graph's legitimate starting points as faults.

questions.chapter: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
questions.question_text: You have written a check for the 32-character label limit. Which calibration set should you run before trusting it on real output?

options.A: The ten candidate graphs, accepting whatever the check reports
options.B: A single 64-character label that is certain to fail
options.C: A good label, a bad label, and labels of 32 and 33 characters
options.D: The longest label found in the published reference book

questions.explanation: Scoring check calibration tests the checks themselves on inputs whose answers you know, before you trust them on real output. A check can pass a bad result or fail a good one, and the second looks like a model failure. The calibration set is small: a known-good input that must pass, a known-bad input that must fail for the right reason, and an edge case at the threshold, such as a label of exactly 32 characters and one of 33.

questions.chapter: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
questions.question_text: In a graph, D needs E, A needs B, B needs C, C needs A, and E needs nothing. The cycle check repeatedly removes every concept with no remaining prerequisites. What is left when it stops?

options.A: Nothing remains, so the graph is acyclic
options.B: Only E remains, because it has no prerequisites
options.C: D and E remain, because they form a single chain
options.D: A, B, and C remain, so the graph has a cycle

questions.explanation: The dependency cycle check repeatedly removes the concepts that have no remaining prerequisites. E needs nothing, so it goes first, and D then has no remaining prerequisite and goes next. A, B, and C each wait on another of the three, so none ever becomes ready. If everything can be removed the graph is acyclic. Here three concepts are left, and they form the cycle, so no order of study satisfies all of them.

questions.chapter: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
questions.question_text: A team scores two models' chapters with an LLM judge and always shows model 1's chapter first. Model 1 wins nearly every comparison. Which weakness of the judge could produce this pattern regardless of quality?

options.A: Position bias: the judge tends to prefer the first candidate
options.B: Data exposure: the judge sends the text to a cloud service
options.C: Calibration: the judge's label limit is set too strictly
options.D: Run variance: the judge was given only one chapter to read

questions.explanation: LLM-as-judge is using a language model to score another model's output. It is fast and cheap, and it is the largest source of bias in this kind of evaluation: a judge tends to prefer text like its own, favors longer answers, is sensitive to the order in which candidates are shown, and rewards confident prose that is wrong. A candidate always shown first can win on position alone. The mitigation is to randomize the order and score twice.

questions.chapter: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
questions.question_text: A reviewer who knows which model wrote each chapter scores the cloud model's chapters higher across many chapters, even when order and length are matched. What is this tilt, and what addresses it?

options.A: Bias from knowing the source; blind review removes the name
options.B: Noise from sampling; more chapters will average it out
options.C: A calibration fault; the check's threshold should be loosened
options.D: Run variance; each model should be run five more times

questions.explanation: Bias in evaluation is a systematic tilt in scoring that favors some results for reasons unrelated to quality. Noise averages out over many runs; bias does not, and it points the same way every time. One named source is knowing the source: a reviewer who knows which model wrote a text, or that it came from a cloud service, is influenced by the name. Blind review, in which the reviewer does not know the model, removes that influence.

questions.chapter: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
questions.question_text: A team must judge the writing quality of locally generated chapters. The text must not leave the site, and the team wants the most trustworthy measure of quality. Which option best meets both criteria?

options.A: A cloud LLM judge, because it scales to thousands of outputs
options.B: A Flesch-Kincaid grade, because a script computes it cheaply
options.C: A single automated score, because it ranks outputs at a glance
options.D: Blind human review against the rubric, in randomized order

questions.explanation: Blind human review is a person scoring output against the rubric without knowing which model produced it, with the order randomized. It is the right test of quality, though slow and costly. A cloud LLM judge sends the text to a service, which undoes the reason for generating locally, and it carries its own biases. A reading-level formula measures form only, and a single automated score hides the profile. Under these two criteria, only blind review qualifies.

questions.chapter: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
questions.question_text: You are asked to design an automated quality score that ranks outputs without hiding where each one is weak, and without defining quality as whatever is easy to measure. Which design meets those requirements?

options.A: A weighted sum of the checks that are fastest to run
options.B: One number that replaces the per-dimension profile
options.C: A score assigned by the same model that wrote the chapters
options.D: A published rubric formula, reported beside the profile

questions.explanation: An automated quality score is a single number a program computes from the checks. It is tempting and dangerous: one number hides the profile, and a weighting that favors the easy checks quietly defines quality as whatever is easy to measure. A sound design is a documented formula over the rubric dimensions, published with its weights, and reported beside the profile, not instead of it. A score from the generating model would add self-preference bias.

questions.chapter: Running the Textbook Benchmark
questions.question_text: What does the benchmark runner do first when it executes a stage?

options.A: Copies the starting directory to a fresh run directory
options.B: Deletes the previous stage's run directory to save space
options.C: Scores the generated files against the written scoring rubric
options.D: Uploads the event stream to the public repository

questions.explanation: The benchmark runner is the script that executes one stage. It takes a model, a label, a prompt file, and a starting directory, and its first act is to copy the starting directory to a fresh run directory. It then starts the harness container, feeds in the prompt and captures every event, stops the run at its time limit if needed, and records the exit code and wall-clock seconds. Because it works on a copy, a run never changes its input.

questions.chapter: Running the Textbook Benchmark
questions.question_text: What happens to a run that reaches its time limit?

options.A: It is restarted from the template with a longer limit
options.B: It continues, and the overrun is recorded only as a warning
options.C: It exits with code 124, and what it wrote so far is kept
options.D: It is deleted, and the model is then removed from the queue

questions.explanation: The run time limit is the longest a run may take before the runner stops it, so a stuck or very slow model cannot occupy the machine for hours. A run stopped by the limit exits with code 124, and what it wrote so far is kept, so a timeout is a result and not a lost run. The limits were 150 minutes for stage 1, 2 hours for stage 2, and 90 minutes for each chapter in stage 3.

questions.chapter: Running the Textbook Benchmark
questions.question_text: Why was Algebra I chosen as the benchmark course?

options.A: It needs MicroSims, a glossary, and quizzes to be complete
options.B: It is the shortest course the skills are able to generate
options.C: A published book gives a scale reference, and reviewers know it
options.D: Its concepts have no dependencies, so stage 1 is simple

questions.explanation: The Algebra I benchmark is this evaluation's instance of a textbook benchmark: the input is a high school Algebra I course description, and the task is its learning graph, chapter structure, and chapter content. The course was chosen for a practical reason. A published Algebra I book already exists, so its size is a reference for scale, and the subject is familiar enough that a reviewer can judge the output without special expertise.

questions.chapter: Running the Textbook Benchmark
questions.question_text: Why does the benchmark use a chapter completion criterion instead of the model's own statement that it finished?

options.A: The model's final message is not saved in the event stream
options.B: A model's claim shows its belief, not what was actually written
options.C: The criterion gives slower models some extra time for each chapter
options.D: The harness cannot detect when the model ends its turn

questions.explanation: The chapter completion criterion says a chapter counts as written when its placeholder text is gone and it has at least 1,000 words. It exists because "the model said it finished" is not evidence. A model that announces completion has told you what it believes, and the criterion tells you what happened. It catches a model that announces it is running a skill and then ends its turn without writing anything.

questions.chapter: Running the Textbook Benchmark
questions.question_text: You are starting stage 2 for a model whose stage 1 run is labeled `s1-<label>`. Which starting directory do you pass to the runner?

options.A: The stage 1 run directory for that model
options.B: The benchmark workspace template
options.C: An empty directory created for stage 2
options.D: The published reference book's repository

questions.explanation: Stage chaining is the arrangement in which each stage starts from the previous stage's output directory, so the work accumulates. The starting directory is the template for stage 1 only; for each later stage it is the previous stage's run directory. The runner copies whatever directory it is given, so the stage 1 output itself is left unchanged. Starting stage 2 from the template would give the chapter-structure skill no learning graph to organize.

questions.chapter: Running the Textbook Benchmark
questions.question_text: A model attempted three stages. Stage 1 ended on its own with all seven required files. Stage 2 ended on its own but left out one required file. Stage 3 was stopped at its time limit. What is its skill completion rate?

options.A: 0 of 3
options.B: 1 of 3
options.C: 2 of 3
options.D: 3 of 3

questions.explanation: Per-stage metrics are defined so that a program can compute them. Skill completion rate is the number of stages that ended on their own with every required file, divided by the stages attempted. Only stage 1 meets both conditions. Stage 2 ended on its own but is missing a required file, and stage 3 did not end on its own because the limit stopped it. The rate is therefore 1 of 3.

questions.chapter: Running the Textbook Benchmark
questions.question_text: In stage 3, the chapter-content skill stops and reports that a chapter's concepts depend on concepts placed in later chapters. Which stage caused the failure?

options.A: Stage 3, because the chapter text was written incorrectly
options.B: Stage 1, because the template was changed during the run
options.C: The runner, because it copied the wrong prompt file
options.D: Stage 2, because its chapter structure ordered concepts wrongly

questions.explanation: The chapter dependency check is a step in the chapter-content skill that verifies each chapter's concepts depend only on concepts in earlier chapters, and it stops the skill when it finds a violation. In three of one model's runs it did so because the model's own chapter structure from stage 2 had placed concepts out of order. The failure appears in stage 3, and the stage that caused it was earlier, which is why chained stages must be diagnosed from the start.

questions.chapter: Running the Textbook Benchmark
questions.question_text: In the worked example, a model's stage 2 produced 14 chapters with 160 of the 200 concepts assigned. What does this imply for stage 3?

options.A: Stage 3 will run faster, because it has fewer chapters
options.B: Stage 3 will fail its strict build on the very first chapter
options.C: Stage 3 cannot cover the 40 concepts no chapter contains
options.D: Stage 3 will reassign the concepts as it writes each chapter

questions.explanation: Each stage starts from the previous stage's output, so a gap carries forward. In the worked example, stage 2 produced 14 chapters with 160 of the 200 concepts assigned, which means 40 concepts were not assigned to any chapter. That limits what stage 3 can write. A per-stage record makes the gap visible at the stage where it arose, before anyone reads the chapter text, which is the reason metrics are kept per stage.

questions.chapter: Running the Textbook Benchmark
questions.question_text: During a queue of runs, the fetch script running with `--watch` stops because a host that had been answering failed twice in a row. What does this most likely indicate?

options.A: The unit has stopped responding and may be frozen
options.B: The book on that unit has finished generating
options.C: The queue reached a model marked with a skip file
options.D: The script deleted the run directory on that unit

questions.explanation: Run output retrieval brings run directories and event streams back to the laptop with `rsync`, which copies new and changed files and never deletes. With `--watch` the script fetches repeatedly and stops when a book or phase finishes, when a host that was answering fails twice in a row, or when no run is going. A unit that has frozen announces itself by failing to answer, so that stop condition is the signal to check on the machine.

questions.chapter: Running the Textbook Benchmark
questions.question_text: A model has timed out on two chapters in a row at 90 minutes each, and twelve chapters remain. Which course of action is best justified?

options.A: Run all twelve, since each chapter is an independent run
options.B: Double the time limit for that model's remaining chapters
options.C: Delete the model's earlier results, since the book is incomplete
options.D: Stop the model and record the remaining runs as not run

questions.explanation: A per-chapter generation run gives each chapter its own timing and limit, and a failure on one chapter does not discard the others. The rule is that a model stops after two time-outs in a row: a model that cannot finish two chapters in 90 minutes each will not finish twelve, and the remaining runs would only occupy the machine. The runs not made are recorded as not run, with the reason. Changing the limit for one model would break a controlled variable.

questions.chapter: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
questions.question_text: What is a text-emitted tool call?

options.A: A call with a wrong name or a missing argument
options.B: A call the harness refuses under a permission rule
options.C: A call written as ordinary text, which the harness does not see
options.D: A call that returns more output than the window can hold

questions.explanation: A text-emitted tool call is a tool call that the model writes out as ordinary text in its reply, in the shape of a call but not as a call. The harness sees no tool call and treats the reply as a final answer, so the run ends. Its signature is a run of one turn whose last message contains something that looks like a call. A call with a wrong name or a missing argument is a malformed tool call, which is usually recoverable.

questions.chapter: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
questions.question_text: Why is a 100% tool-call success rate on 28 calls not necessarily better than 84% on 50 calls?

options.A: A success rate is meaningful only above 100 tool calls per run
options.B: Failed tool calls are never recorded in the run's event stream
options.C: A higher call count always means a more careful model
options.D: The 28 calls may never have reached the file-writing step

questions.explanation: The tool call count, the failed tool calls, and the success rate all come straight from the event stream, and a number alone does not diagnose. 100% success on 28 calls is not better than 84% on 50 if the 28 calls never reached the step that writes the file. The count is the prompt for a question, and the event stream holds the answer: what the calls did, and whether the work was finished.

questions.chapter: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
questions.question_text: Why does an evaluation report put the method before the recommendation?

options.A: A reader needs the method in order to judge the recommendation
options.B: The method is the shortest part and is the quickest to read
options.C: The recommendation cannot be drafted until the report is printed
options.D: The method lists the limitations, which must always come first

questions.explanation: A report structure is the order of an evaluation report's parts: question, method, results, limitations, recommendation. The order matters because each part answers a reader's question in turn. A reader who meets the recommendation before the method has nothing to judge it with, and a report that puts limitations after a confident recommendation has buried the part that tempers it. Limitations are their own part, placed before the recommendation, not inside the method.

questions.chapter: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
questions.question_text: A model's three benchmark stages take 4 hours. With the three stages set at 10% of the work of a whole book, what is the whole-book time estimate?

options.A: 4.4 hours
options.B: 40 hours
options.C: 14 hours
options.D: 400 hours

questions.explanation: A whole-book time estimate extrapolates from the measured stages. The three benchmark stages were set at 10% of the work of a whole book, so the estimate is the three-stage time divided by 0.10: 4 hours ÷ 0.10 is 40 hours of machine time. The figure rests on an assumption about stages that have not been run, so treat it as a model to adjust. If the three stages were 5% of the book, the estimate would double.

questions.chapter: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
questions.question_text: A 13-chapter book costs $52.92 to generate, and 8 of its chapters meet the completion criterion. What is the cost per usable chapter?
questions.explanation: Quality-adjusted cost corrects the cost for how much of the output is usable. One way to express it is the cost per usable chapter: the generation cost divided by the chapters that met the completion criterion. Here $52.92 ÷ 8 is about $6.62. Dividing by all 13 chapters gives $4.07, which prices chapters that were never written. A cheap model that leaves chapters unwritten is more expensive per chapter than its speed suggests.

questions.chapter: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
questions.question_text: Every model you try fails at the first turn with the same "model not found" error. What should you do before concluding anything about the models?

options.A: Record that none of the models can run the skill
options.B: Raise the time limit and rerun every model once more
options.C: Compare each model's peak context with its window
options.D: Check the base address, model name, and mounts first

questions.explanation: Harness misconfiguration is a fault in how the harness was set up and not in the model: a wrong address, a model name the server does not have, a skill folder that was not mounted, or a permission rule that stalls. Its signature is a failure at the very first turn, for every model, with an error that names the configuration. A failure identical across all models is a configuration fault until shown otherwise, so check the setup before blaming any model.

questions.chapter: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
questions.question_text: A run's final message says the chapter skill is now running. No tool call follows, and no chapter file exists in the run directory. Which cause does this evidence point to?

options.A: Premature turn termination: work described but not done
options.B: Malformed tool call: an argument had the wrong type
options.C: Context overflow: the conversation exceeded the model's window
options.D: Harness misconfiguration: the skill folder was not mounted

questions.explanation: Premature turn termination is the model ending its turn before the work is done, with no error. Its signature is a final message that describes work and no file that contains it. Here the model announced the skill, made no tool call, and wrote nothing. A malformed call would show an error and usually a retry, context overflow shows late forgetting with a peak near the window, and a misconfiguration fails at turn one for every model.

questions.chapter: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
questions.question_text: The cost model assumes the three benchmark stages are 10% of a whole book. If they are really 5%, how does the cost per textbook change, and why?

options.A: It halves, because fewer stages remain to be run
options.B: It doubles, because the whole-book hours double
options.C: It is unchanged, because the yearly cost is fixed
options.D: It rises by 5%, matching the change in the share

questions.explanation: The cost per textbook is the whole-book hours times the cost of a generating hour. The whole-book hours come from dividing the measured three-stage time by the share of the book those stages represent. Halving that share from 10% to 5% doubles the whole-book hours, so the cost per book doubles, from about $53 to about $106 in the reference case. The yearly cost is fixed, but it is spread over half as many books.

questions.chapter: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
questions.question_text: One model completes all three stages, the cost is estimated at $53 per book, and no human review has been finished. Which sufficiency statement is best supported by this evidence?

options.A: The DGX is sufficient, because one model finished every single stage
options.B: The DGX is insufficient, because no human review has been completed
options.C: The DGX is sufficient, because $53 is below any service price
options.D: Completion is established, cost is estimated, quality is unknown

questions.explanation: A DGX sufficiency judgment answers whether this machine, with these models and this harness, is enough to generate the textbook. It is a judgment made against criteria written down beforehand: completion without an unusable fault, acceptable time and cost, and reviewed quality that meets the standard. The honest answer can be that the first is established, the second is estimated, and the third is not yet known. Declaring the machine sufficient or insufficient outright claims more than this evidence shows.

questions.chapter: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
questions.question_text: Local models complete the learning-graph and chapter-structure stages, the chapter-text stage exposes capability differences, and every result is one run with no finished human review. Which recommendation design fits this evidence?

options.A: Local for every stage, stated as a final verdict
options.B: Cloud for every stage, since one stage showed weakness
options.C: A provisional hybrid routed by stage, with its conditions stated
options.D: No recommendation until each model has been run five times

questions.explanation: A recommendation is the action the evidence supports, stated with its conditions. When local models complete the structural stages and a hard stage exposes differences, the rules lean toward a hybrid routed by stage: structural stages local, a stronger model for the prose. Because every result is one run and no human review is finished, the recommendation must be labeled provisional and say what would change it. A flat verdict or a refusal to recommend both serve the reader worse.

questions.chapter: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
questions.question_text: What is the goal of sanitization, stated in terms of the reader?

options.A: The reader learns the method and findings, not how to reach the machine
options.B: The reader can reproduce the run on the same physical machine
options.C: The reader sees every raw log in full, with only the passwords taken out
options.D: The reader can verify each result by logging in to the device

questions.explanation: Sanitization is the process of removing or replacing the details in an artifact that could identify, locate, or give access to a device or a person, so the artifact can be shared. The goal is stated in terms of the reader: someone who reads the artifact should learn how the evaluation was done and what it found, and nothing that makes the tested machine easier to find, reach, or log in to. It is a pipeline step with its own checks, not a final polish.

questions.chapter: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
questions.question_text: What are documentation address ranges?

options.A: Addresses that a tailnet assigns to its member devices
options.B: Addresses that home routers give to devices behind them
options.C: Addresses that a scanner skips when it reads a repository
options.D: Addresses reserved so that examples never point at a real machine

questions.explanation: Documentation address ranges are blocks of addresses reserved so that examples never point at a real machine. When an example needs an address that looks concrete, use one of them, such as `192.0.2.0/24` or `198.51.100.0/24`. A placeholder in angle brackets is clearer for a name, and a documentation range is clearer for an address that must still parse as one. A fake value that looks real is worse, because someone will eventually try it and a scan cannot tell it from a leak.

questions.chapter: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
questions.question_text: Why must a serial number be redacted even though it grants no access?

options.A: It can be used in place of a password at the SSH login prompt
options.B: It identifies the physical unit and ties the document to it
options.C: It reveals which ports are open on the machine's firewall
options.D: It lets a stranger join the tailnet without needing an invitation

questions.explanation: Hardware identifiers are values that identify a physical unit: serial numbers, GPU unique identifiers, and network card addresses. They are not secrets that give access, but they are identifying details that tie a document to one machine. A serial number sits in a system file on the machine, and a GPU's identifier is printed by a common command, so both slip into captured output easily. Open ports and firewall rules are a different category, access configuration.

questions.chapter: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
questions.question_text: Why does this project keep raw run output in a directory outside the repository?

options.A: Nothing has to be removed, because it never entered the repository
options.B: The repository has a size limit that run logs would exceed
options.C: Git cannot store files that are written in JSON lines format
options.D: The logs must stay on the DGX so that the Administrator can read them

questions.explanation: Raw output isolation is keeping unsanitized output in a place that is never published, so that nothing has to be removed from the repository because it never entered it. In this project, run output lives under a directory in the home folder, outside the repository, and only a script that copies selected, safe files can bring anything in. This matters because git history persists: a file that was committed once stays readable in earlier commits.

questions.chapter: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
questions.question_text: You are sanitizing a status line that shows a tailnet address, the machine's full name, the administrator's account, and a remote endpoint that must still read as an address. Which replacements follow the book's conventions?

options.A: Invented values that look realistic, for all four of the fields
options.B: `100.x.y.z`, `<dgx-host>`, `<admin>`, and a documentation-range address
options.C: A blur over all four fields in a screenshot of the terminal
options.D: The real tailnet address, since it works only from inside the tailnet itself

questions.explanation: Redaction replaces a detail in a specific artifact with a placeholder or removes it. Following the conventions, the tailnet address becomes `100.x.y.z`, the full name becomes `<dgx-host>`, and the administrator's account becomes `<admin>`. The remote endpoint takes an address from a documentation range, because a placeholder there would not read as an address. Invented realistic values are worse than placeholders, and a tailnet address still names a specific device in a specific network.

questions.chapter: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
questions.question_text: You need a screenshot of a terminal for the report. Which steps should you follow?

options.A: Crop first, cover with a solid fill, then check at full size
options.B: Blur the prompt, then shrink the image so that details are small
options.C: Keep the full window, and cover only the password line
options.D: Capture the whole screen, and rely on the secret scanner

questions.explanation: Screenshot redaction removes identifying details from an image, which carries more than the lines you meant to show: window titles, tab names, and a prompt with the username and hostname. Three rules cover most of it. Crop first, to the smallest region that makes the point. Cover with a solid fill, not a blur, because a blur can be partly reversed. And check the result at full size, including the edges, where a prompt line is easy to miss.

questions.chapter: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
questions.question_text: A repository passes a `gitleaks` scan with no findings, yet a figure caption in a chapter contains the machine's hostname. Why did the scanner miss it?

options.A: The scanner reads only the files listed in `.gitignore`
options.B: The `--redact` flag removed the hostname from the report
options.C: The scanner checks only the commits older than the current one
options.D: A hostname in prose has no credential shape for it to match

questions.explanation: Secret scanning runs a tool over files or history that looks for strings with the shape of a credential, and gitleaks has built-in rules for the common key and token formats. A scanner finds credentials with a known shape. It does not find an IP address in a paragraph or a hostname in a caption, so it is one layer and not the whole defense. A person's publication safety review exists to catch what patterns cannot.

questions.chapter: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
questions.question_text: A log file was committed last week. Today you add `*.log` to `.gitignore`, but git still tracks the file and its changes. Why?

options.A: The pattern must list each log file by its full name
options.B: The `.gitignore` file applies only to the deployed site
options.C: A gitignore does nothing for a file that is already tracked
options.D: The pre-commit scan re-adds any files that match its patterns

questions.explanation: Gitignore rules list patterns that git will refuse to add, so a careless `git add .` cannot pick up a log. A gitignore is a safety net and not a control. It does nothing for a file that is already tracked, and it will not stop an explicit `git add -f`. The committed log also remains in the repository's history, so adding the pattern afterward neither untracks the file nor removes what was already recorded.

questions.chapter: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
questions.question_text: A log excerpt has had every hostname and address replaced, yet it still reveals an account name on dozens of lines. Where is the name coming from?

options.A: The model tag that appears on each line of the run log
options.B: The documentation-range addresses left in the excerpt
options.C: The version numbers of the driver and the server
options.D: The home directory paths on lines that touch a file

questions.explanation: A home directory path is a file path that begins with a user's home directory, and it carries the username. A run log shows `/home/<user>/...` on every line that touches a file, so a single excerpt can reveal an account name dozens of times even after hostnames and addresses are gone. Replace the home directory with a placeholder, or prefer paths relative to the project root, which carry no account at all.

questions.chapter: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
questions.question_text: An access token was committed and pushed to the public repository an hour ago. Which response is best justified?

options.A: Delete the file in a new commit and push it at once
options.B: Rewrite history with a force-push and tell no one
options.C: Stop, tell the repository's owner, and rotate the token
options.D: Add the file's pattern to `.gitignore` and carry on

questions.explanation: Git history persistence means a commit stays in history after a later commit removes its content, and clones, forks, and the deployed site keep their own copies. So the order of operations is fixed: stop and tell the person responsible for the repository, and do not try to hide the leak with a quick follow-up commit. Treat the credential as compromised and rotate it, because removing it from history does not un-expose it. Rewriting history is a last resort.
